###### 1. INTRODUCTION 

Coral Bay Nickel Project is owned by Coral Bay Nickel Corporation (CBNC), which is a joint venture between Sumitomo Metal Mining Company Ltd. (SMMC), Sojitsu Corp., Mitsui & Company, Ltd., and Rio Tuba Nickel Mining Corp (RTNMC).  SMMC has developed the flow sheet to treat stockpiled limonite, a type of laterite ore, that was previously considered as mine waste by RTNMC. It is located at Barangay Rio Tuba, municipality of Bataraza in the southern part of Palawan Island, Philippines.  The new plant applying the flow sheet was constructed and commissioned in the later part of 2004. 

The mechanical works of the Rio Tuba Plant were completed in August 2004.  After the completion of the commissioning in March 2005, commercial production started in April 2005.  The plant has been on a ramp-up schedule since then, gradually increasing its production rate of mixed sulfide. The production rate has reached the design capacity at the end of 2005 and exceeded the design in the early part of 2006. 

###### 2. CORAL BAY NICKEL PROJECT

###### 2.1. CORAL BAY NICKEL PROJECT 

Coral Bay Nickel Corporation (CBNC), which is a joint venture company of Sumitomo Metal Mining Co. Ltd. (SMMC) and other shareholders, will produce Nickel/Cobalt Mixed Sulfide (MS) from lowgrade limonitic ores employing the new technology called  High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL), at Rio Tuba, located in southern Palawan Island, Philippines. The plant is designed to produce 10,000 metric tons of nickel and 750 metric tons of cobalt annually, as mixed sulfide. 

The raw materials are stockpiled mine wastes at the Rio Tuba Nickel mine site which was then considered as inadequate material for the production of ferronickel. Rio Tuba Nickel Mining Corporation (RTNMC) was established in 1969 and has exported saprolite ore to Japan as a raw material for the ferronickel production since 1977. During the operation, the limonite ore, which was located above the saprolite ore body, has been stockpiled separately according to nickel content and silica-magnesium ratio. The Rio Tuba stockpiles contain 21 million dry metric tons, averaging 1.26 % nickel and 0.09 % cobalt, sufficient to maintain the annual production of 10,000 t Ni for 20 years. 

###### 2.2. PROJECT INPLEMENTATION 

SMMC dispatched the first technical mission to Rio Tuba in the early part of 2000.  It can be seen in Figure 1 that the first production of mixed sulfide was in December 2004.  It is noteworthy that CBNC has realized the first nickel product after only 5 years from the time when the project was initiated.  After the preliminary investigation, the board of SMMC decided to proceed with the bankable feasibility study and simultaneously, other tasks like environmental assessment and metallurgical tests were undertaken in July, 2000. 

After the feasibility study was completed in July 2001, the board of SMMC approved the project. All the statutory requirements for the construction and operation were secured.  The major government permits included the Environmental Compliance Certificate and Mineral Processing Permit.  The ECC was granted by the Department of Energy and Natural Resource in July 2002, and the MPP in September 2004.  The project was registered at PEZA in December 2002 and was granted tax incentives.  Construction work started in the early part of 2003. 

Basic engineering design of the project commenced in January 2001.  The metallurgical tests were conducted twice at Dynatec Corporation in 2001 and Lakefield Research Limited in 2002.  In addition to these studies, pilot tests of the process were conducted at Niihama Nickel Refinery of SMMC between July 2001 and March 2002.  These studies finalized the plant design at Rio Tuba. The EPC contract was agreed in August 2002 with JGC Corporation.  The mechanical works were completed in August 2004.  Part of the pre-commissioning work was carried out since June 2004 and the activities were completed in mid-November 2004.

Figure 1. Project Implementation The Filipino operators newly employed were extensively trained and educated for one year at Niihama Nickel Refinery of SMMC in Japan. They have transferred to Rio Tuba since the precommissioning. The first acid injection was conducted on 19 November 2004. The first mixed sulfide was produced on 26 December 2004. The test works were conducted until mid-April 2005. The main objectives include confirmation of the maximum flow rate and establishment of the reaction control. CBNC announced the commencement of commercial production on 14 April 2005 with an inauguration ceremony. Although there were some problems such as water shortage caused by a drought and mechanical trouble at the power plant, CBNC has gradually increased its production rate. The production rate of MS has reached the design capacity in late 2005 and exceeded the design since mid-February 2006. ###### 3. CONCEPT OF PLANT DESIGN The Coral Bay Project was a strategic investment and challenge for SMMC. The aims of the project are to establish HPAL technology and to minimize the initial capital. Based on these aims, the principal policy including 10,000 t Ni production capacity, acid importation and production of mixed sulfide were adopted. The mixed sulfide is processed at Niihama Nickel Refinery by the proven technology of MCLE (Nickel Matte Chlorine Leach Electro winning). The policy has led to the establishment of a technology producing high purity nickel from low grade laterite ore. A conscientious investigation of the existing HPAL plants clarified difficulties attributed to the design and the plant practice. Heavy duty of pumps and valves and poor control system of HPAL circuits were pointed out as the major issues in the engineering design. Meanwhile, the scale control method, lack of experienced workers, and requirement for highly skillful operation were found also as key issues in the plant practice. The new design overcoming these difficulties has been finalized. The training program of the operato

rs was carefully selected and then implemented at Niihama Nickel Refinery and at Rio Tuba HPAL Plant. Development of the operation software was extensively conducted in the hot water commissioning stage of the plant. 3 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au It is noticeable that the basic design of the plant includes counter measures to worst scenarios such as insufficient capacity of filtration and shortage of retention time for chemical reactions. Subsequently, additional tank space and possible conversion of filters to improved designs were considered as the proper counter measures. ###### 4. COMMISSIONING OF PLANT The clear target is important in the commissioning stage. Therefore, the commissioning was divided into sub stages in the Coral Bay Project. Those sub stages are the following: July -Nov. 2004 Nov.-Dec. 2004 Jan. - Feb. 2005 Feb. - Apr. 2005 Apr.- Aug. 2005 Aug - Oct. 2005 Oct. - Dec. 2005 Hot Water Commissioning: Training and brushing up SOP Solution Fill Up: Confirming the condition of chemical reactions Maximum Flow Rate: Finding bottle neck in liquid and gas flow Product Quality: Establishing reaction control methods Continuous Operation: Operation for a month at 70% flow rate Maximum Production Rate: Finding bottleneck in the plant Name Plate Capacity: Finding bottleneck at higher production rates Figure 2 shows the operational history of the plant. Since the mechanical completion, unscheduled shut down of the plant accounts for almost 200 days. Half of that is due to engineering and construction defects and the rest is attributed to failures in the operation. A turning point can be seen in August 2005 when the operation days exceeded the unscheduled shut down. This indicates the completion of punching the defects. After the first major maintenance shut down from September to October 2005, the unscheduled shut down has been reduced considerably. Figure 3. Production rate of mixed sulfide A major trouble occurred at the power plant in August 2005. The power plant consists of 11 MW turbine generator and coal fired boiler with a capacity of 105 t/h steam generation. Heavy rains continued for one week from end-July to early-August. It damaged the coal conveying system of the boiler and the emergency power generators, eventually resulting to a complete blackout. However, the plant continued to operate even during the drought and monsoon rains and the flow rate of HPAL circuit was gradually increased to the maximum. As a result, MS production corresponding to 80 % of the design capacity was achieved in the middle of August to the middle of September 2005. In September 2005, the first maintenance shut down was conducted and major modifications in the plant were carried out. The production rate of mixed sulfide has reached at the design value in the end of 2005 and exceeded the design in March 2006. The Coral Bay Project has progressed very well. The successful ramp-up activity was attained in a fast track record. The achievement suggests that design allowance for the worst scenario is very essential and this seems to be strongly dependent on the experience of plant practice. SMMC has superior experience of hydrometallurgical operation. A strong leadership for quick decision is also a key to the success. The commissioning team was fully supported by SMMC and authorized to implement the large scale modification. During the stage of solution fill up, the commissioning team found many problems such as insufficient power of agitators for the chemical reactions. Some of them were issues of the worst scenario. The corrective measures were immediately considered and the modification or the mitigation plan was undertaken within 2 months. This indicates that the experience in nickel production and the speedy movement led to the successful commissioning of the Coral Bay Project. 5 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### 5. CONCLUSION The production ramp up of the HPAL plant has been successfully achieved in the Coral Bay Project. The project was planned in 2000, and the plant construction and equipment installation was completed in August 2004. The first acid injection was conducted in middle of November 2004 and the production rate reached almost the design level in the end of 2005, or after just about one year since that time. Furthermore, the plant has already produced nickel at more than 1000 t/month, exceeding the design capacity, in the early part of 2006. This success can be attributed to a thoughtful plan, a flexible design of the plant, and a strong team to implement the commissioning work. ###### 1. ABSTRACT 

The Gladstone Nickel Project (GNP, or ‘the Project’) is currently undertaking a definitive feasibility study (DFS), due for completion in late 2006.  The Project’s nickel and cobalt refinery (the ‘Yarwun refinery’) is to be located at the major Queensland coastal port of Gladstone to capitalise not only on the infrastructure in the vicinity, but also on the extensive high grade laterite resources available from the South West Pacific.  Open pit mining at GNP’s wholly owned Marlborough deposits will produce ores principally for beneficiation, which will then be pumped as slurry to the Yarwun refinery for processing to metal.  Marlborough ore supply will be complemented by imported ores, which will be delivered in Capesize ships and conveyed 5km directly into the Yarwun refinery from the Central Queensland Port Authority’s (CQPA’s) new Wiggins Island Coal Terminal (WICT). Timing of the Project is such that: 

- recent experience and innovations in high pressure acid leaching (HPAL) related technologies, and 

- skilled personnel from the design, construction, commissioning and operation of 2<sup>nd</sup> and 3<sup>rd</sup> generation HPAL plants 

can be utilised to develop a 4<sup>th</sup> generation refinery at Gladstone that will be able to operate for many decades as a major, leading edge, nickel and cobalt producer. 

###### 2. INTRODUCTION 

Gladstone Pacific Nickel Ltd (GPNL) was listed on the London Stock Exchange’s Alternative Investment Market (AIM) on 17 March 2005. 

The GNP comprises the Marlborough mine and Coorumburra ore preparation plant to be located 30km to the south of Marlborough, Queensland, and the Yarwun refinery, to be located in the Gladstone State Development Area (GSDA), Queensland.  The Coorumburra ore preparation plant will be connected to the Yarwun refinery by a 175km pipeline, pumping ore slurry from Marlborough to Gladstone as shown in Figure 1.  The proposal to locate the Yarwun refinery in Gladstone is consistent with the importation of overseas ore to complement the Marlborough resource and facilitate the development of a long life project.  The Aldoga residue storage facility (RSF) will be located in the Aldoga precinct of the GSDA, approximately 14km from the Yarwun refinery. 



Figure 1.

Location of the Marlborough mine, Yarwun refinery and RSF. 

The Marlborough resources that are being initially focussed upon contain 125 million tonnes, grading 0.8% nickel.  Within these resources, comprising the Slopeaway, Coorumburra and Whereat deposits, GPNL has defined a resource in terms of JORC measured and indicated

categories of 52.5 million tonnes, grading 0.93% nickel (at 0.7% nickel cut-off grade) and 0.06% cobalt. 

During 2005 extensive geological drilling was undertaken with a view to increasing the resource on the basis of measured and indicated categories.  In addition to the resource definition drilling, 12 off 900 mm diameter holes were drilled, using a Calweld bucket rig, to obtain bulk samples representative of the projected first 5 years’ mine operation.  A selection of intervals from the Calweld drill holes was then dispatched to SGS Lakefield Oretest (Oretest), in Perth, Western Australia, for metallurgical testwork. 

A key to the project is the beneficiation of the Marlborough resource material, with batch and pilot plant testwork being undertaken at Oretest in late 2005, adding to the database initiated by Preston with its testwork conducted at Ammtec in 1998 and 1999.  Representative blends of Marlborough material were prepared in the beneficiation pilot plant for HPAL piloting. 

The Yarwun refinery flowsheet (Figure 4) is based on the application of the HPAL process and sulphide precipitation to produce an intermediate mixed sulphides product (MSP).  The MSP will subsequently be leached, with nickel and cobalt metal being recovered in hydrogen reduction and formed into briquettes. 

The location of the Yarwun refinery in Gladstone takes advantage of the readily available infrastructure required for the project and minimises transport costs associated with the movements of bulk materials such as ore and sulphur.  In addition, the town of Gladstone has a long and successful history in the implementation and operation of complex process plants. 

###### 3. HISTORY 

The Gladstone Nickel Project was commenced by the Pearce Matheson Group Pty Ltd (PMG) in 2003, which was seeking to acquire the entire issued share capital of Marlborough Nickel Pty Ltd (MNPL) from Preston Nickel Holdings Pty Ltd (Preston). 

By the end of 1999 Preston had spent approximately A$30 million acquiring property and tenements at Marlborough and completing a Bankable Feasibility Study (BFS) to develop a stand-alone nickel laterite project at the Marlborough mine.  The project was subsequently shelved, mainly due to the difficulties being experienced at the time with the commissioning and operation of the Bulong project, which Preston had purchased from Resolute Resources Ltd in 1998.  PMG began discussions with Preston and its bankers, Barclays, in 2001 leading to the acquisition of MNPL, the owner of the Marlborough deposits, by GPNL on 29 December 2003. 

In mid 2003, PMG commissioned the fir

st of two scoping studies for the GPNL project.  These were both undertaken by Aker Kvaerner Australia (AKA), which is part of one of the world’s leading engineering groups with recognised expertise in the fields of nickel laterite processing technology and engineering.  The first study focussed primarily on the concept of importing ore to a plant sited at Gladstone.  The second study, completed in August 2004, focussed on developing the initial stage of the project (Stage 1a) using ore supplied by a mine at Marlborough, with ore importation planned to commence after the successful commissioning of that Stage. 

Following the listing of GPNL on AIM on 17 March 2005, an owners’ team of experienced professionals has been assembled to manage the various sub-consultants and undertake a definitive feasibility study (DFS).  Most GPNL team members have substantial and directly relevant nickel industry experience with companies such as Queensland Nickel, Western Mining, BHP Billiton, Black Range, Preston Resources and Anaconda Nickel. 

GPNL’s main specialist consultants include:

- Environmental Impact Assessment at Yarwun and Aldoga – URS 

- EIS and tenure of slurry pipeline – Resource & Land Management Services (RLMS)

###### 4. GEOLOGY 

The Marlborough resource is located approximately 30km south of the township of Marlborough and approximately 75km northwest of Rockhampton in Queensland, Australia.  The Marlborough resource is easily accessed via the Bruce Highway and adjacent established roads.  Grid power and water is available in the vicinity to support the proposed mining, ore preparation and slurry pumping operations. 

MNPL, a wholly owned subsidiary of GPNL, owns 12 mining leases totalling approximately 7,560 hectares which provide secure tenure over the Marlborough mine deposits.  Six exploration permits (EPM) comprising 102 sub-blocks covering over 30,000 hectares almost totally surround the mining leases.  The Queensland Department of Natural Resources, Mines and Energy administers all tenements. 



Figure 2.  Marlborough resource tenement map. 

The Marlborough nickel resource is contained within a laterite that overlies the Princhester Serpentinite.  The Princhester Serpentinite lies in the northern part of the New England Orogen and has been described as the largest ultramafic mass in Eastern Australia (Murray, in prep 2006). Originally, the Princhester Serpentinite consisted of harzburgite, minor dunite and clinopyroxenite that have been partially or completely serpentinised (Bruce e

t al, 2000). 

At the Marlborough nickel laterites there is little evidence of the original lithologies, with serpentinite, often veined with magnesite, outcropping in stream beds and low lying areas.  Chromitite pods and lenses occur sporadically in the area.  Mafic dykes intrude the serpentine and recent mapping has shown these to trend mainly NNE and NW (Humphries 2006). 

Page 4 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 

A number of laterite bodies (Figure 2), listed from North to South, are preserved in the Marlborough area: 

- Woodstock 

- Slopeaway (includes Gumigil East) 

- Coorumburra (East, West and Central) 

- Surfers 

- Magpie (East and West) 

- Kurrawong 

- Wattle Hill 

- Whereat (previously called Junction) 

- Moores 

- Lagoon Hill 

The laterites occur on elevated topography and the laterite profiles are more fully preserved on the higher elevations, such as at Slopeaway.  Of the laterite bodies listed above, four have been extensively drilled and form that current resources base (in bold). 

The laterite profile was divided (Martin 2006) for resource evaluation purposes and based on chemical and physical characteristics, into four “domains”, from top to bottom these are: 

- Ferruginous Zone –  high in iron and aluminium and often containing bands of silcrete; 

- • Upper Saprolite – lower in iron and low in magnesium (0.5 – 6%) and is variably silicified often producing conchoidally fractured drill chips; 

- Lower Saprolite – is higher in magnesium (6 – 15%) and often contains clay; and 

- Basement – the high magnesium serpentinite. 

It is recognized, that from a geological perspective more domains are present in the profile, however, the above proved adequate for geological modelling and resource estimation. 

###### 5. MINERAL RESOURCES 

The mineralisation of the Marlborough resource deposits and the exploration areas extend for over 40km.  Known resources are contained within ten separate areas that were the subject of various programs of resource definition drilling by BHP Billiton and INCO between 1964 and 1973 and subsequently by Preston in 1997 and 1998. 

The four initial Marlborough deposits, being Slopeaway, Coorumburra (East and West), and Whereat (previously called Junction), were upgraded to JORC Code resource category by Preston after completing a comprehensive program of drilling, metallurgical test work and financial modelling.  This work formed the basis for the BFS conducted by Preston in 1997 and 1998. Estimates produced during the BFS showed that the Marlborough deposits contained Measured, Indicated and Inferred mineral resources of approximately 96.1 million dry tonnes with an average grade of 0.79% nickel and 0.05% cobalt at a cut-off grade of 0.7% nickel equivalent (Ni Eq<sup>2</sup> ). 

In 2005 GPNL undertook a 27,000m drilling program managed by International Mining Consultants (IMC) of Brisbane.  The main aim of the program was to infill areas on Slopeaway and Coorumburra to increase the l

evel of confidence in the resource estimate to an Indicated level, and to extend, in areas of potential, the current deposits.  A further objective was to investigate deposits that Preston did not drill. 

The program was successful in that the Measured, Indicated and Inferred mineral resources were increased from 96.1 million dry tonnes grading 0.79% nickel and 0.05% cobalt to 125 million dry tonnes grading 0.8% nickel and 0.05% cobalt, using similar cut-off grades<sup>3</sup> .

###### 6.1 Flowsheet 

Unlike Preston, who proposed a mixed hydroxide precipitation (MHP) based flowsheet for metal production at Marlborough, GPNL proposes an MSP based flowsheet for metal production at Gladstone.  There are advantages and disadvantages associated with both flowsheet options, and ultimately, depending on project partner preferences, either route can be catered for (as can the additional alternatives of intermediate production for refining elsewhere, if necessary).  As the capital and operating costs associated with both processing routes are sufficiently similar, the flowsheet decision at this stage has been based on intangible, project specific factors such as technology track record and availability of skilled personnel in Glad

stone. 

The flowsheet proposed for the GNP is presented in summary format in Figure 4 and is based on the original Marlborough flowsheet incorporating the precepts of Atmospheric Leaching as tested by Calliope (Faris et al 1997). 

While this flowsheet can be considered somewhat conventional, engineering and testwork activities take advantage of the lessons learned by our predecessors to maximise nickel refining capacity. 

###### 6.2 COORUMBURRA ORE PREPARATION PLANT 

The flowsheet development activities for the Marlborough resource are premised on minimising mass recovery, while achieving financially optimal nickel grade and recovery in beneficiated materials.  As a result, the Marlborough resource definition was revised to incorporate two subresources: 1) Low magnesium saprolite (LMS), to be processed in the HPAL autoclaves and 2) High magnesium saprolite (HMS) to be processed in the Saprolite Neutralisation circuit.  This approach has re-defined the value of HMS, which was previously considered waste by Preston, into a material with the potential to add value to the GNP as a substitute for the neutralising capacity of limestone.  The added benefit of the HMS resource is the nickel and cobalt credits obtained in the Saprolite Neutralisation circuit.

The basis for selection of this was the trade off between minimising capital and operating costs and solution inventories containing hydrogen sulphide. At a lower operating pressure, and with the number of vessels which would then be required for the Project, it was anticipated that the operational difficulties associated with the precipitation of mixed sulphide onto the surfaces of the vessels and interconnecting pipes would require GPNL to install a wholly redundant parallel circuit thereby leading to increased capital investment. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

The late 1990’s saw the development of three laterite nickel plants in Western Australia in which the fundamental design of the pressure acid leach (PAL) was fashioned after the autoclave technology developed from the pressure oxidation (POX) gold plants in the United States and Canada. All of the nickel leach plants were designed and constructed by different engineering companies with previous experience in developing POX plants. Consequently the plants, although similar, had subtle differences that made them operate differently with varying degrees of success.

The development of the Rio Tuba pressure acid leach (PAL) plant stemmed from the experiences gained from the preceding operations. This paper will discuss the definition of 2nd generation design, and the advances in design that were made at Rio Tuba as a result of the experiences of previous operations; The paper will expand on the collaborative approach by the owners Coral Bay Nickel Corporation (CNBC), the EPC contractor JGC Corporation (JGC) and the HPAL designers SNC-Lavalin Australia (SLA) in developing the design and minimising the risk in the project.

###### **1.2.2 Further Process Development** The pressure acid leach route was further developed by Amax in the 1970's. Although Amax never proceeded to commercial production, this work made a major contribution to the longer term development of the technology. Amax selected the pressure acid leaching route for its Prony Project in New Caledonia in the 1970’s, and embarked upon an extensive pilot-scale test program to improve and further develop the process used at Moa Bay. Amax were the first to adopt multi-compartmental horizontal autoclaves, with mechanical agitation of each compartment. At pilot scale, improved mixing patterns, compared with Moa Bay, tended to reduce scale growth. Scaling was f

urther reduced by staged addition of acid into the first few compartments.  Improvements in materials for pressure letdown chokes enabled the recycling of steam to a series of pre-heaters, which reduced steam consumption by up to 60%.  The original Moa Bay sulphide precipitation step was improved by using seed recirculation to reduce operating pressure and temperature, which lowered capital cost and decreased scaling. Although the Prony plant was never built, the Amax work, which was widely published, made a major contribution to the longer term development of the technology.

###### **1.2.4 Flowsheet Options** 

Each of the three plants constructed in Western Australia adopted significantly different approaches to the flowsheet selection, influenced by the nature of the ores, and the quality of available process water, which varied between saline and hypersaline, influencing the process and materials of construction. - Murrin Murrin partially follows the Moa Bay flowsheet for the leach plant with a Sherritt developed refinery, precipitating the metals as sulphides, re-dissolution with oxygen under pressure followed by solvent extraction and hydrogen reduction, to produce nickel and cobalt briquettes and ammonium sulphate;

Whilst all use high pressure acid leach (HPAL), all adopted different approaches to the autoclave design and more particularly the design of the flash and heater trains. ###### **4.2.1 Ore Processing Characteristics** 

This design is influenced by the nature of the lateritic ore to be processed. Key factors are: 

- Mineralogy 

- The amount of variability within the ore body 

- The competent nature of the ore for upgrading and sizing. 

- The quantity of sulphuric acid consuming minerals 

- Scale formation 

SMMC performed extensive testing of the stockpiled ore to determine variability and characteristics for processing. Batch and pilot testwork was undertaken by Dynatec Corporation during 2001, and also during 2002 by Lakefield Research Limited.  SLA assisted in the interpretation of the testwork and the development of the design criteria. Both the combination of atmospheric leaching (ATML) and high pressure acid leaching (HPAL) were investigated, with batch and pilot work test runs. The ATML was investigated as a means to treat the

saprolite ore component utilising the residual acid content from the HPAL discharge, therefore reducing the cost of neutralising using Limestone. 

The stockpiled ores were categorised by predominately limonite ore, low grade soft ore (LGSO), and high iron ore (HFO). 

Key to this area was the determination of the blending methodology, parameters, and rheological requirements, for the feed density, acid consumption and ORP (oxidation reduction potential) operating and design ranges for the autoclave.  Feed densities of 45% were able to be achieved and were used as a design basis; however the design needed to be able to operate over a range of densities and rheological conditions, a common issue in previous plants. 

In addition to these studies, pilot tests of the process were conducted at Niihama Nickel Refinery of SMMC between July 2001 and March 2002.  The stockpiled ore leant itself to being processed and blended utilising drum washers and high pressure spray vibrating screens. The use of river water, low in salt and carbonates, and the ore being low in silica and magnesium contributed to high feed densities and low acid consumption, and low expected scale formation. Heater scale was expected to be a mixture of anhydrite and haematite caused by calcium saturation of the process water and acid/slurry carry-over from the flash vessel.  In the autoclave, scale was expected to be haematite and hydronium alunite/jarosite with minor quantities of silica. Rates of scaling depend on the supersaturation of iron, aluminium and silica, which in turn depend upon the mineralogy, pulp density, acid addition, temperature and water salinity. Design and good control of acid addition, flash vessel carry over and autoclave mixing are required.

ent and Material Performance** 

The nickel laterite HPAL plant is a high pressure, high temperature plant, with highly acidic (sulphuric acid) slurries and depending on ore and water quality varying levels of chlorides. The ore typically contains aluminium and magnesium which tend to form scale in acidic conditions and can contain hard chromites compounding erosion. Both oxidising and reducing conditions can exist, complicating the material selection. Also the act of removing scale can contribute to the problems with damage to the lining. 

The HPAL plant utilises high cost materials such as titanium, super duplex steels, ceramics, coatings and bricks to combat the severe erosion/corrosion conditions. The cost of the HPAL plant design is driven by amount and application cost of this material to be installed and the ability to maintain this equipment. This influences not only the equipment design, but the layout of the HPAL area particularly in optimising piping quantities and accessibility for maintenance.

###### **4.2.2.1 Autoclave Feed Pump** 

High temperature feed pumps were first applied for the pressure oxidation gold plants. These pumps were called “Heat Barrier Design” pumps or more commonly drop leg designs and utilised inlet and outlet “cone” check valves.  The fundamental difference for the operation of the autoclave feed pumps in the laterite plants as compared to POX gold plants is a much higher operating temperature and pressure. It is these two factors that have lead to a considerable redevelopment of the autoclave feed pump for HPAL applications. 

The typical  POX autoclave feed pumps operate between 165 to 175ºC with design discharge pressures of about 2200 kPa while the laterite HPAL feed pumps operate over 190ºC with design discharge pressure exceeding 5600 kPa. Like the POX autoclaves, the HPAL circuits are designed to maximize heat recovery to save on live steam requirements but operate at much higher temperatures and pressures. 

Due to the HPAL operating conditions, titanium materials were used in the pump valves and accumulators in contact with the slurry.  This posed problems for manufacturers testing the limit of the casting size of the cone valves and the housings. 

Even with the titanium materials it was expected that valve life would be low compared to the POX operations and valve life was conservatively estimated at 400hrs. Consequently both Bulong and Murrin Murrin specified 100% capacity pumps in order to achieve high throughput capacity without any effective loss of capacity. Cawse’s pumps were sized at 80% capacity with the normal operation of two duty pumps. All

three operations have double acting duplex pumps. 

Soon after commissioning is was found that the MTBF (mean time before failure) of the cone valves was much shorter than had been anticipated and transient pressure pulsation through the pump affected the pump performance. 

In actual operation the pumps were plagued with low valve life and poor availability. Cycle times of the PD pump valves were as low as 50 hrs with the rubber elastomer cone valves and high undampened pressure spikes through the drop leg and wet end severely impaired pump performance. 

The PD pumps at Rio Tuba can be considered an evolution in pump design and specification standard for the high temperature application such as HPAL. The Rio Tuba pump is a single acting triplex pump designed with titanium metal seated cone valves. 

The metal seated valves are a departure from the traditional rubber elastomer designs and were first developed at Murrin Murrin during operation. In the early development of the valves uptime was not consistent but was considered to be a marked improvement over the rubber elastomer design, the chloride levels limit their application. Further development has led to valves that consistently achieve over 2000 operating hours. 

The single acting triplex significantly reduced the undampened pressure pulsation thereby improving the pump performance. After commissioning had taken place at Rio tuba the pressure pulsations were not detectable.

The steel shell of the autoclave is lined typically with a layer of corrosive resistance material (titanium), allowing the steel to be protected whilst maximising the process volume of the vessel in comparison to brick lining. The sizing of the Autoclave is driven by the retention time to ensure the extraction of the nickel and cobalt. All autoclaves built for the WA laterites were from the same manufacturer.

The autoclave agitators in the Western Australian laterite plants all suffered from varying levels of material (corrosion and stress cracking) and seal failures and agitation mixing deficiencies. The agitators and associated seals were not purpose built for the application, but were a combination of agitator vendor, seal manufacture and seal systems coupled together.  In particular with the seals they had to deal with high pressure and temperature differentials and acid conditions, which again tested the experience from the POX applications. 

Critical failures occurred in the areas of suitable titanium grade components, agitator seal alignment, and the supply of flush and barrier fluids to the sealing faces with automatic back up systems.  Modelling and design development of the mixing efficiency and power requirements of the agitators in HPAL conditions have improved following these failures. 

###### **4.2.2.4 High Pressure Flash Vessels** 

The three Western Australian operations have all had problems with operation of the high pressure flash tanks, including high vent velocities, erosion of valves, failures of brick lining and control valves/blast tubes.

Carry over of acid slurry from the vessel leads to erosion of lines, and scaling and corrosion in the heater train. Due to the high velocities (momentum) generated in the pressure let down of the autoclave discharge slurry, the HP flash vessels are designed with a pool of liquid to absorb this momentum, as well as impingement blocks/bricks to protect the brick lining at the bottom of the flash vessel.  The maintenance of this pool is critical, and the discharge of the HP flash is controlled be side overflow discharge and level control on the downstream flash vessel inlet valve. If the level drops too low the vessel may be damaged, if it is too high this can lead to excessive carry over through the vapour lines at the top of the vessel. 

The sizing of the flash vessels is a balance between the cost of installation versus the erosion and corrosion cost, and downtime from upstream scaling in the heater circuit. Vent lines are sized to cater for upset conditions of high velocity solids and acidic carry over and are made from titanium, and designed to minimise erosion, including the provision of hardening of pipe bends. 

The feed density into the autoclave and operating pressures of the flash vessel are critical to control, as low density and pressures lead to large increases in the volume of vapour required to be vented, entraining slurry in the process. These variations will be encountered in the commissioning and operation of the laterite plants and need to be taken into consideration. 

The control of level in the flash vessel is particularly difficult with the disturbed surface and hig

h temperature acidic slurry challenging most conventional contact and remote level measurements. Nucleonic sources are used in this application.  Due to the thickness of the lining these radioactive sources, and associated housings, are large and require particular design attention in supply, and installation.

Rio Tuba utilises a wet scrubber with inlet spray bars for coalescence, cyclone scrubber with recycle spray condensing similar to the Bulong plant. 

###### **4.2.2.7 Layout Design** 

The HPAL plant utilises high cost materials such as titanium, super duplex steels, ceramics, and coatings to combat the severe erosion/corrosion conditions. The cost of the HPAL plant design is driven by amount and application cost of this material to be installed and the ability to maintain this equipment. This influences the layout of the HPAL area particularly in optimising piping quantities and accessibility for maintenance. 

Access includes providing space and facilities for: 

- descaling of strainers, piping and equipment, 

- replacing of high wear area bends 

- removal and inspection of autoclave discharge, flash and heater control valves and relief valves 

- removal and replacement of autoclave agitator seals 

- drainage and descaling of the autoclave, feed pumps and heaters 

- brick repairs of flash vessel train

Lessons learnt from the operations allowed the identification of high operator access and maintenance areas, and the provision of structure and equipment necessary to perform this. This allowed the design to cater for crane, hoist and platform access whilst keeping the layout tight, reducing capital cost of the plant. The medium temperature (MT) and High Temperature (HT) heaters were designed as stacked heaters, minimising plot space and titanium line lengths and fittings, but also had to be designed to allow for access for scale cleaning with suitable platform and height allowances particularly into the bottom of the HT heater. 

###### **4.2.2.8  Piping Design** 

All the piping in the HPAL area must be designed for the design pressures and temperatures of the associated equipment as well as allowances for erosion and corrosion, and scaling.  Due to high cost of the material there is a balance between the material selection, the ultimate thickness, and layout design and the cost of repair/change-out of lines. Significant corrosion has occurred in the existing WA laterite plants when they were commissioned in the heater train and the HPAL discharge where duplex and super duplex steels and rubber lining have been installed, in an effort to reduce capital costs. 

The wear on pipes is predominantly at elbows, “T’s, Y’s” and downstream of control valves and hence repairs are usually concentrated in these areas. In particular process lines in vent duty see particularly high wear when compared to slurry lines. 

In the existing WA laterite plants some lines are patched several times before replacement while other operators immediately order a replacement as soon as one fails so that a replacement will be ready the next time that lin

e fails. Titanium pipe lines that are replaced are Page 21 of 24 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au kept so that subsequent repairs can be made for other lines. Often a failed 90° elbow can be cut into a useable 45° elbow for instance. Stub ends can usually be saved and sent to the fabricator to form the replacement pipe that has been order. Techniques such as the “weld hardening” of bends have been used successfully to reduce time between repairs. The three nickel laterite plants in Western Australia (Cawse, Bulong and Murrin Murrin) although related have different experience in terms of which lines wear the most. This is largely due to difference the HPAL design (the number of stages in heating and flashing) and engineering factors the designer allowed for the lines and of course the layout of pipe the lines, as well as the ability of the plant to operate within the design range of the plant. Adequate sizing and flanging to allow for this repair and slurry descaling is critical to the availability of the HPAL plant. ###### **4.2.2.9 Operability and Maintainability of Plant and Utility Systems** Shutting down and starting up of the plant can compound the erosion/corrosion of the plant and also the dislodgement of scale and blockage of equipment and piping. Issues from cycling the plant include: - Stressing of the brick lining of vessels leading to spalling or failure of the brick lining - Scale dislodgement for equipment leading to blockages in piping and pumping systems. - Stress on dissimilar metal components - Changing reducing/oxidising conditions in the titanium clad vessels. - Erosion of valving seats and plugs from increase cycles of closing and opening. Maintenance during operations will need to address the following issues: Critical to the maintenance of the HPAL are: - Supply chain and spares storage for speciality items - A minimum/maximum spare part system - Specialty repair facilities for valve and agitator seals. - High pressure cleaning systems for descaling, - Trained alloy/Ti welders on site - Condition monitoring systems Page 22 of 24 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### **5.0 CONCLUSION** The HPAL flowsheet, although complex and operating at high pressures and temperatures in highly corrosive and erosive conditions, has been demonstrated to be able to be designed and operated successfully. PROJECT OVERVIEW The Rio Tuba HPP (Hydrometallurgical Processing Plant) project involved the construction of a process complex to produce nickel and cobalt from stockpiles at Rio Tuba Mine, Palawan Island, Philippines. The plant is designed to produce 10,000 tons of nickel and 750 tons of cobalt per year, as mixed sulfide, for 20 years. The process is designed to produce Nickel/Cobalt Mixed Sulfide (MS) at a high recovery rate by the HPAL method using low grade ore and limonite as the raw materials, which are stockpiled at the RIO TUBA MINE as non-eligible materials for production of ferronickel. The intermediate material (Nickel/Cobalt mixed sulfide) is shipped to Niihama Nickel Refinery of Sumitomo Metal Mining Co., Ltd. in Japan and is further processed to electrolytic nickel and cobalt, respectively, by the Sumitomo technology. 3 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### 2.2. ###### 1. INTRODUCTION 

###### 1.1. PROJECT OUTLINE 

Coral Bay Nickel Corporation (CBNC), which is a joint venture company of Sumitomo Metal Mining Company (SMMC) and other shareholders, will produce Nickel/Cobalt Mixed Sulfide (MS) from low-grade lateritic ore and limonite by a new technology, including High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL), at Rio Tuba, located on southern Palawan Island, Philippines.  The plant is designed to produce 10,000 metric tons of nickel and 750 metric tons of cobalt annually as mixed sulfides. 

The raw material of low-grade lateritic nickel ore and limonite are mine wastes stockpiles at the Rio Tuba Nickel mine site.  Rio Tuba Nickel Mining Corporation (RTNMC) was established in 1969 and has mined and exported saprolite ore to Japan as a raw material for the ferronickel production since 1977.  During that operation, the limonite ore, which was located above the saprolite ore body and consid

ered as an inadequate material for the production of ferronickel, were stockpiled separately according to nickel content and silica-magnesium ratio. 

The Rio Tuba stockpiles contain 21 million dry metric tons, averaging 1.26 % nickel and 0.09 % cobalt, sufficient to maintain the annual production of 10,000 t Ni for 20 years.  Commissioning of the plant was carried out in the latter part of 2004.  Commercial operation officially started in April 2005.  The intermediate product or mixed sulfides of nickel and cobalt will be shipped to SMMC’s Niihama Nickel Refinery (NNR) in Japan, where it will be further refined to electrolytic nickel and cobalt by the proven Matte Chlorine Leach Electrowinning (MCLE) technology of SMMC. 

###### 1.2. LOCATION 

Palawan Island is located in the South China Sea and is 425 kilometers long and 50 kilometers wide. The Rio Tuba Nickel Mine is located at the southern tip of the island. The location map of the Rio Tuba Mine is shown in figure 1. 



Figure 1.  Location map 

###### 1.3. PROJECT HISTORY 

SMMC and RTNMC agreed to undertake joint investigations on the stockpiled Rio Tuba lateritic nickel ore in April 2000, and the pre-feasibility study was completed in July 2000.  An innovative process to produce a mixed sulfide precipitate from the lateritic ore was proposed in this study. Following the highly encouraging pre-feasibility study, SMMC conducted a bankable feasibility study, and this has led to the establishment of Coral Bay Nickel Corporation (CBNC) in 2002. 

###### 2. PROCESS DISCRPITION 

###### 2.1. PROCESS FLOW 

The flow sheet of this process is shown in figure 2. 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 1 

The overall processing scheme consists of the following steps 

- Ore Preparation 

- High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) 

- Pre-Neutralization (P-NTRL) 

- Counter Current Decantation (CCD) 

- Neutralization (NTRL) 

- Zinc Removal (De-Zn) 

- Sulfurization (MS) 

- Final Neutralization (F-NTRL) 

###### 2.1.1. Ore Preparation 

The ore preparation stage consists of shakeout machines, drum washers, vibrating screens, and a thickener. At first, ore over 100mm is rejected using the shakeout machines.  Secondly, ore under 100mm is fed into drum washers where with water sprays, the ore agglomerates are broken up and the plus 25mm materials are removed.  Finally, the ore under 25mm goes to the vibrating screens from which the minus 2mm particles are obtained. The plus 2mm part joins the earlier oversize.  The screening is carried out with high pressure water sprays.  The slurry containing the ore under 2mm is transferred to a thickener.  The concentration of solids in the thickener is controlled at 45%. 

###### 2.1.2. High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) 

The objective of the high pressure acid leach stage is to extract nickel and cobalt selectively from the ore by using sulfuric acid.  The reaction is carried out at a temperature of 245 degrees C and a  pressure of 4 MPa. The retention time is 60 min.  As

a result, about 95% of nickel and cobalt is leached while the extraction rate of iron is only about 3%. 

The HPAL operation is carried out in an autoclave with 6 compartments, where pre-heated slurries are fed and high pressure steam and sulfuric acid are also injected.  The steam recovery system consists of 3-stage flash tanks that recycle the excess steam to the 3-stage pre-heaters.  The ore slurry is heated up to 100 degree C in the first heater by the steam recovered from the third flash tank.  The temperature of the slurry gradually increases to 158 degree C in the second heater and 208 degree C in the third heater.  The steam recovered from the second flash tank is injected into the second heater, and the steam from the first flash tank is injected into the third heater. The leached slurry is discharged to the flash tanks and then to the preneutralization stage. 

###### 2.1.3. Pre-Neutralization (P-NTRL) 

The objective of the pre-neutralization stage is to neutralize excess free acid in the pregnant solution of the slurry.  Limestone slurry is added as the neutralizing agent.  The reaction is carried out for 45 minutes at about 100 degree C until a pH of 1.0 is attained.  The neutralized slurry goes to the 7-stage Counter Current Decantation (CCD) circuit. 

###### 2.1.4. Counter Current Decantation (CCD) 

The role of these CCD thickeners is to separate the pregnant solution from the leached residues by counter current washing using mainly barren liquor from the sulfurization stage introduced at the last thickener.  The underflow slurry from the last thickener is discharged to the final neutralization stage at high solid density, The amount of nickel and cobalt which are present as an adhered solution in the underflow slurry is already insignificant.  On the other hand, the pregnant solution which is the overflow of the first thickener is transferred to the next neutralization stage. 

ln normal operation, CCD wash stages operate as follows.  The underflow slurry containing the leach residue from the previous stage thickener (n - 1) is mixed with the overflow solution from the following stage (n + 1) in a mixing tank, and then transferred into the thickener.  In CCD 7 thickener, the barren solution from the sulfurization stage is added as wash solution to CCD 6 underflow slurry in the mixing tank 7 before transferring to CCD 7 thickener.  Flocculant is dosed into the thickeners to improve settling characteristics of the leach residue.  Solid% of the underflow slurry is at more than 40%. 

The underflow in the neutralization thickener(discussed in the next paragraph) is transferred to CCD 3.  The neutralized residue is washed by acidic solution in the CCD circuit together with the leach residue from the HPAL stage.  The washed underflow slurry is discharged to the final neutralization stage from CCD 7.  This circuit is operated at 70-80 degrees C and at a pH of 1.0 to 2.0.  The rather low pH is maintained to carry out settling while pre

venting the precipitation of nickel. 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 2 

###### 2.1.5. Neutralization(NTRL) 

The objective of the neutralization stage is to remove impurities, such as iron, aluminum, and chromium, by precipitating them as hydroxides.  The pregnant solution from CCD 1 thickener is transferred to the first neutralization tank.  Limestone slurry is added into the tank and reaction is carried out at about 60 degrees C with pH adjusted to 3.2-3.4. The leached residue from CCD 2 underflow is added to the tank as a seed to improve settling characteristics.  The addition of the leach residue effectively prevents scale formation in the tank.  The retention time is 90 minutes. 

The neutralized solution is transferred to a thickener.  The underflow slurry from the thickener is discharged to CCD 3 for further recovery of nickel and cobalt in the precipitate, while the overflow solution is transferred to the zinc removal stage. 

###### 2.1.6. Zinc Removal (De-Zn) 

The objective of the zinc removal stage is to remove zinc in the solution from the neutralized stage. If zinc remains in solution, it will co-precipitate with nickel and cobalt in the sulfurization stage and contaminate the final mixed sufide.  The presence of zinc in the mixed sufide creates a problem in the electro-winning cell during the final refining at Niihama Nickel Refinery in SMMC. 

The solution after the neutralization stage is pumped to the zinc removal reactor.  Zinc is precipitated as zinc sulfide selectively by hydrogen sulfide gas (H2S).  Co-precipitation of nickel and cobalt is controlled to <0.1 % for nickel and <0.3 % for cobalt. 

The reaction pH is maintained in the range of pH 3.0-3.4.  The retention time is 60 minutes under a slight pressure of less than 10 kPa.  The zinc content is reduced to less than 1 mgpl.  At the same time, copper is also removed completely.  The slurry is filtered by polishing filters.  The zinc sulfide is repulped with water and discharged to the final neutralization stage.  The solution is transferred to the sulfurization stage. 

###### 2.1.7. Sulfurization(MS) 

The objective of the sulfurization stage is to recover nickel and cobalt as an intermediate product. The zincfree liquor is transferred to the sulfurization tank.  Nickel and cobalt are precipitated as Ni/Co mixed sulfide (MS). 

The zinc-free solution is heated up to 70-80 degree C by steam.  The solution containing nickel and cobalt is reacted with hydrogen sulfide gas (H2S) in the range of pH I.5 and 2.0.  Over 99 % of nickel and cobalt is recovered as mixed sulfide.  Impurities such as manganese and magnesium remain in the solution.  The pressure is controlled at 200 to 300 kPa.  Recycling of MS seed enables better  control of the MS particle size and minimizes scale formation on inside surface of the reactors.  The retention time is 60 minutes. 

The product slurry is discharged to a thickener.  The underflow from the thickener is fed to a pressure filter. A

fter the elimination of the hydrogen sulfide gas in the solution, the mixed sulfide slurry is washed and dehydrated by pressure filters, while the barren solution is recycled to the CCD stage as washing solution. The excess of the barren solution is discharged to the final neutralization stage.  MS product from the pressure filter is packed in flexible containers. 

###### 2.1.8. Final Neutralization (F-NTRL) 

The objective of the final neutralization stage is to remove the remaining heavy metals such as manganese, iron, and chromium in the barren solution and to adjust pH of the solution to be suitable for discharge to the sea.  The heavy metals and the trace amount of acid are precipitated as hydroxides and gypsum with limestone slurry and lime slurry.  The barren solution from the sulfurization stage is recycled to CCD 7 as washing solution.  Only excess barren solution is discharged to the final neutralization stage.  The underflow slurry from the CCD stage is the main stream discharged to the final neutralization stage. 

The underflow slurry in the CCD thickener and the barren solution are transferred to the first tank. There are four tanks in series in the final neutralization stage.  The reaction is carried out for 120 minutes at about 70 degrees C.  Limestone slurry is added to the first tank, and free acid in the solution is neutralized to pH 6.0. Lime slurry is added into the second and third tanks, and heavy metals are precipitated as hydroxides with pH increased to 8.0.  The neutralized slurry is discharged to the tailing dam.  The solid contents of the slurry settles and cools at the tailing dam.  On the other hand, the supernatant portion is directly discharged to the sea through a 12 km long pipeline.

###### 3.1.2. Scale Formation in MS Stage 

Two HPAL plants presently operated by Moa Bay<sup>5</sup> and Murrin Murrin<sup>6</sup> have adopted sulfide precipitation for primary concentration of nickel.  Both plants prefer relatively high temperatures in the sulfide precipitation reaction.  The purpose of high temperature operation is high recovery of nickel and fast kinetics.  In the Coral Bay process, lower reaction temperatures of 70-80 degree C are employed. 

Slow kinetics are preferred for preventing scale formation in the reactors, and a longer retention time is required for high nickel recovery at the lower temperatures of 70-80 degrees C.  There is no significant difference in capital cost between both operations.  However, the operating cost of low temperature operation is lower than that of high temperature operation.  Therefore, test work was carried out in benchscale and pilot-scale equipment to study the prevention of scale formation and the achievement of high nickel recovery. 

The test work has indicated that the reaction temperature is in the range of 70-90 degrees C for the desirable nickel recovery<sup>7</sup> .  The recycle of mixed sulfide as seed has been found effective to prevent the scale formation on surface of the reactors.  A fine particle size of MS is preferable for this purpose.  Based on this development, a portion of the mixed sulfide precipitate is ground and recycled to the reaction vessels in the plant practice. 

Inspection showed scales less than 1 mm on the MS reactor surface, which indicates no need for de-scaling work.  The same conditions are now applied in the plant.  It was proven that adequate seed recycle and low reaction temperature minimized the scale formation. 

###### 3.1.3. Scale Formation in Neutralization Stage 

The seed recycle of leach residue has been developed by SMMC to prevent scale formation in the neutralization tank.  It was also proven in actual plant practice.  The formation of gypsum scale is effectively prevented.  Nickel loss accompanying neutralization precipitate is almost negligible. 

###### 3.2. CONTROL OF ACID LEACH 

There are important parameters learned in the extraction of nickel and iron from the ore in the HPAL plant practice.  The nickel extraction was found to be dependent on free acid concentration in the leach solution, while the dissolution of iron from the ore is affected by the oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) in the leach solution.  The ORP can be controlled by proper blending of the ores. The content of carbon and sulfur influences the ORP.  Thus, the ore blending method is designed according t

o the content of carbon and sulfur. A high pressure air compressor was installed to supply air to the autoclave to maintain favorable ORP range. Proper ore blending successfully resulted in high nickel extracton rate, and depression of the iron concentration in the leach solution in actual plant practice. It is necessary to maintain acid concentration at equal to or more than 47 gpl in order that nickel extraction is achieved at more than 95 %. As the average of free acid concentration is controlled at 48 gpl, nickel extraction rate could be maintained at 95.4 %. The relationship between ORP and iron concentration in the leach solution is shown in figure 6. The iron concentration decreases with increasing levels of ORP. The solution pH in the CCD thickeners increases gradually as it flows forward, and the pH in the final thickener is sometimes close to 3. Aluminum is precipitated at pH greater than 2. It is well known that nickel co-precipitates with some metals like aluminum. Thus, operation of the CCD stage at pH less than 2 is preferable to minimize the nickel loss. In the Coral Bay process, the washing solution fed to the CCD stage is the barren solution from the sulphurization stage. The pH of the barren solution is maintained around 1.7 to 1.8. When the barren solution is added to CCD 7, the pH of CCD 7 thickener is maintained at less than 2. This operation effectively prevents co-precipitation of nickel in the CCD stage. It also accelerates the dissolution of any nickel co-precipitated with the impurities in the neutralization stage. Steam recovery system in the HPAL stage The carry over of leached slurry with steam from the flash tanks to the heaters has a big influence on the corrosion of the equipment in HPAL stage, especially the heater feed pumps and autoclave feed pump. Therefore, the proper control method of steam recovery is important. A new monitoring system of the flash tank level has been developed and installed during the pre-commissioning. The carry-over test was implemented in September, 2004. Na2SO4 was used as a trace

r to establish the control method. It was seen that carry-over is proportionate to the flow rate of the discharged slurry from the autoclave. The operating pressure of the flash tank has been found to affect the carry over. The rise of pressure increases the carry over. The high pressure flash tank (HP) is normally operated at the pressure between 1.7 and 1.8 MPa. The carry over from HP flash tank is greater than that from the medium pressure flash tank (MP) and low pressure flash tank (LP) which are operated at pressures between 110-600 kPa. Na2SO4 was added at the suction of the autoclave feed pump by another pump with a fixed flow rate. Carry over was computed from SO4 concentration which was calculated from flow rate in each flash tank and SO4 concentration which was actually measured in each heater. The relationship between carry over and flow rate of feed slurry to the autoclave is shown in figure 9. Furthermore, the level of slurry in the flash tank is also an important factor to determine the carry over. Tests were undertaken at different levels of 25 %, 50 %, and 75 % with LP flash tank as shown in figure 10. The operation with low slurry level effectively prevents the carry over. However, it is possible that the impingement block that protects the bottom of the flash tank may be damaged when the level in the flash tank is controlled too low. Therefore, at present, the level of HP flash tank and MP flash tank is controlled at 35 %, the level of LP flash tank at 20 %. The condition of the impingement block is monitored and there are no indications that may lead to serious damage so far. 10

CONCEPT OF TURN DOWN AND CATCH UP OPERATION It is important to provide for turn down operation or the catch-up operation in case of troubles and to reduce the shutdown times in order to increase the plant availability. ration are as smooth as possible and that the risk of the plant shutdown is little. The capacity in each stage in the plant is shown in table 5. To provide for turn down operation and catch-up operation, there are two trains in the ore preparation stage which have the capacity of 84 % per train. A similar concept was proposed for the leaching of base/precious metal polymetallic sulphide ores and/or concentrates [5]. In 2005, after a relatively limited amount of testwork, Jaguar Nickel made a decision to defer any further development of these processes [6,7] and it has, therefore, been left to others to investigate whether there is ultimately any potential in this approach. Jervois Mining Limited (JRV-ASX) of Melbourne, Australia [8] has 100% ownership of the Young Laterite Deposit in New South Wales. Although this is generally a relatively low-grade deposit, it is extremely well-situated with local communities nearby, has a tappable gas pipeline running across the site, a magnesite mine next door, and, importantly, all of the necessary land usage rights negotiated and signed. Various preliminary invest

igations carried out by Jervois indicated that processing of the resource by more conventional means (PAL, HPAL or atmospheric sulphuric acid leaching) did not appear to be economic, and its low grade ruled out any of the pyrometallurgical options.  Subsequent scoping tests then indicated that atmospheric chloride brine leaching appeared to offer some possibilities for the processing of the Young laterite materials and consequently, significant additional testwork has been undertaken to determine the feasibility of a chloride-based process. 

As the process has evolved, there has been an appreciably greater understanding of the controlling parameters such that the now-envisaged flowsheet is not only significantly different from that originally conceived by Jaguar Nickel, but it is also one wherein the recovery of value-added products for Ni, Co and Mn, as well as for iron, can be contemplated. 

This paper discusses some of the major premises which resulted in the concept of the Jaguar Nickel Process, demonstrating the limitations that now necessarily follow, although these were not readily apparent when the process was first proposed, and traces some of the newer developments in high-concentration chloride leaching.  Results of laboratory leach tests are presented for various feed materials, but with emphasis on those achieved for the Jervois Young laterite.

The source of the nickel/cobalt mineralisation is the Wambidgee Serpentinite of Cambrian age. The serpentinites (originally harzburgites) have intruded the Jindalee Beds in elongate north-south bodies associated with faulting.  Regionally the serpentinites are mapped from Grenfell in the north to Tumut in the south, a distance of 150 kilometres.  In the Young/Cootamundra area, they are flanked on the eastern side by the Silurian, Young Granodiorite.  It is believed that this is an important factor in the formation of the mineralised laterites.  Run-off in the region is from east to west (from the Great Dividing Range) and the acid-rich ground water, after traversing the 30-kilometre wide granite belt, has chemically leached the basic composition of the serpentinites, removing silica, magnesium and other soluble

A feature of the laterisation is that there are at least two eras of weathering with repeated (hematite)/limonite/saprolite horizons.  Since the hematite horizon is less enriched in nickel and cobalt, there is frequently a middle (and sometimes upper) zone of low-grade material separating the run-of-mine mineralisation.  A further feature is that the mineralisation can spread laterally across the underlying serpentinite/granite contact. 

###### **3 LATERITE CHLORIDE LEACH PROCESSES** 

###### **3.1 PUBLISHED CHLORIDE LEACH PROCESSES** 

There are no operating plants using chloride for laterite feeds, although a number of potential flowsheets have been both proposed and/or investigated.  BHP Minerals (as it then was) developed a chloride-based heap leach process [9], in which nickel and cobalt were recovered from the chloride leach liquor via ion exchange, or via precipitation with recycled magnesia from pyrohydrolysis.  Iron was either precipitated, also with recycled magnesia, or itself subjected to pyrohydrolysis after solvent extraction.  These methods of dealing with iron, whilst perfectly technically feasible, seem to require large quantities of recycled magnesia, and therefore do not appear to be viable economically because of the high energy costs associated with the pyrohydrolysis method of generating it. 

A somewhat similar process has also been proposed by Gibson and Rice [10], in which iron is removed by solvent extraction and pyrohydrolysis, and magnesia also by pyrohydrolysis.  No data were provided on this circuit, since the focus of the paper was on the solvent extraction of nickel with Versatic 10.  However, whilst the solvent extraction process may be technically feasible, extracting such large quantities of iron generates a significant amount of acid which still has to be neutralized, again usually by recycled magnesia, prior to the recovery of nickel and cobalt, and which, as noted above, does not appear to be viable economically. 

Other chloride-based circuits have been proposed by Nichromet Solutions Inc. for the recovery of nickel and cobalt amongst other metals [11,12,13].  The first circuit proposed is somewhat complex, and proposes the control of iron by relatively low temperature selective spray roasting of the solution, after the addition of potassium chloride (to stabilize the ferrous iron and magnesium), wherein the iron will be converted to hematite.  Other metals, such as magnesium, nickel and cobalt, contained in the product are then recovered and removed by washing (water leaching) the hematite residue, since they remain in the chloride form.  If, as is quite likely, some of the magnesium forms its oxychloride, otherwise known as “Sorel Cement,” then it will not be possible to wash this magnesium out of the hematite, since the oxychloride is markedly insoluble.  A more recent variation [13] of this process [11] essentially simply

evaporates the chloride leach solution containing magnesium, iron, nickel, cobalt and chromium to dryness, maintaining the temperature of evaporation between 130-180°C, and removing the water and HCl in a stream of air.  At these temperatures, it is claimed that the addition of KCl is not necessary, iron is converted to Fe2O3 and chromium to Cr2O3, with the other metals remaining as their respective chlorides.  Although the energy costs compared to spray roasting will be less, the solids still have to be re-leached (washed) with water to recover the paymetals.  It is also certain again that some magnesium forms either its oxide or oxychloride in this operation; were it not so, the problems with oxide formation suffered by every single electrolytic magnesium metal producer would not exist.

Recently, Intec Limited described what also appears to be a somewhat complex new chloride-based process wherein the limonite fraction of a laterite is leached by hydrochloric acid in a solution of calcium and sodium chlorides [14].  The process can be operated in either one or two stages, the first stage being at 100-110°C and the second, or if it is just a single-stage process, at 150-220°C in an autoclave.  In this process, both dissolved iron and magnesium are precipitated via the use of lime, iron as hematite and magnesium as MgO.  The process also requires the substantial addition of sulphuric acid to regenerate the hydrochloric acid from the resulting calcium chloride solution, with the sulphate balance being controlled by the further addition of lime.  The use of an autoclave and the large requirement for sulphuric acid seem to mitigate against the use of this process, and unless a saleable form of calcium sulphate can be produced [15,16,17], there will also be a considerable residue fall. 

Generally in these processes, iron is oxidised to its ferric state (if necessary) and then precipitated with a base, usually magnesia for laterites and lime for sulphides.  It has also been proposed (there are no plants doing so) to recover the ferric iron by solvent extraction followed by pyrohydrolysis.  A recent proposal for controlling iron is to form FeOOH, either β-FeOOH (akaganeite), α-FeOOH (goethite), or a mixture thereof [18].  However, if akaganeite is formed, then it will contain a significant chloride component (as high as 7% Cl), leading to both chloride losses and consequent difficulty in satisfactorily disposing of the residue.  Even this approach requires the addition of a base, but it is based to some extent on controlled supersaturation precipitation [19], which produces a more uniform and crystalline material and is far more attractive than, for example, the turboaeration process proposed by Great Central Mines in their chloride copper process [20]. 

###### **3.2 JAGUAR NICKEL PROCESS (ACLP)** 

When first presented, it seemed that Jaguar Nickel’s Atmospheric Chloride Leach Process (ACLP) might be abl

e to overcome some of the problems inherent in the hydrometallurgical processing of nickel laterite ores.  The publications from Jaguar Nickel [1,2,3,4] as well as the patent application [21] show that one of the two key original concepts of the high-concentration chloride laterite leaching circuit was the simultaneous (or, more correctly, sequential) leaching and precipitation of iron in the leach reactors, using the properties of the concentrated magnesium chloride brine matrix and the inherent alkalinity of, particularly, the saprolite fraction of the ore.  This was intended to permit a very low addition rate of hydrochloric acid to be used at no higher than 150 kg/tonne dry laterite [4]. 

Combined with this leaching approach, hydrochloric acid was to be regenerated via pyrohydrolysis of magnesium chloride liquor after nickel and cobalt recovery.  Since pyrohydrolysis is an energy-intensive process, the process as described by Jaguar could only be economic if the amount of solution requiring pyrohydrolysis was kept to a minimum, and therefore the acid consumption was kept low.  It would appear from their news releases [6,7] that Jaguar was unable to control either the extent of magnesium leaching, or of maintaining the acid addition at reasonable levels,<sup>a</sup> and therefore that any further work on the development of the process was discontinued.

###### **4 PROCESS FUNDAMENTALS** 

###### **4.1 ACID ADDITION** 

Laterite ores tend to be highly variable in nature, not only from deposit to deposit, but also within any given area of any specific orebody.  This has especially been the case with the response to leaching in strong acidic chloride brines.  Experience has shown that some laterite samples readily release their contained nickel and cobalt, and thus perform as expected in a Jaguar-type circuit, with low acid addition resulting in both high metal extraction and final solution iron levels <1 mg/L.  Other samples have been much more refractory, requiring significantly higher levels of acid addition to attain acceptable metal extraction. Alternatively, if final solution iron levels <1 mg/L were to be achieved, it also led to appreciably reduced recoveries of nickel and cobalt because of the tendency of the goethite/spinel/hematite precipitate to coat, and hence passivate, the unleached particles of laterite. 

This unpredictable and variable behaviour prompted a re-evaluation of the fundamentals of such a process, with the result that the Jaguar concepts have been abandoned for the new projects currently being evaluated.  The leach conditions are now designed to take all of the iron, and hence all of the associat

ed nickel, cobalt and manganese, into solution, in a leach circuit such as that shown below in Figure 1. Such a process, therefore, is able to handle all types of laterite ore. This requires significant amounts of hydrochloric acid to dissolve the iron, and, of course, is completely contrary to the “accepted practice” of minimal acid addition. Furthermore, even though higher acid additions are used, the net amount of magnesium that leaches is potentially reduced, because the magnesium content of the ore is no longer used as a base for the precipitation of the iron. The new approach would not be economically feasible if all of this acid had to be regenerated by either of the pyrohydrolysis approaches mentioned above. The new flowsheet concept, then, is inconsistent with the original Jaguar Nickel concept of employing pyrohydrolysis as a means of regenerating the lixiviant, since the energy costs would be prohibitive. The reason why it is possible to use such a high acid consumption in the current flowsheet is due to the unique properties associated with high-strength chloride brines, and more importantly, with high concentration magnesium chloride. These properties are the concentration of iron, concentration of magnesium and the associated vapour pressure of hydrochloric acid (hydrogen chloride). There is a very brief discussion of these properties at the end of this paper. It is beyond the scope of the present paper to give more than a brief outline; a much more detailed discussion of the iron control and lixiviant regeneration circuit will be presented in October, 2006 [22]. ###### **4.2 LIXIVIANT MATRIX** The properties of chloride systems are well known [1,2], and the chlorides of calcium, sodium and magnesium can, in theory, equally be used. Mixtures of calcium and sodium chlorides have both been proposed and been used commercially [14,23], and could be applied in the present context. Calcium is equally effective as magnesium in promoting laterite leaching, and both are slightly more effective than sodium. With magnesium chloride, however, the extent of magnesium dissolution is significantly less than it is with calcium, where ultimately, a calcium-magnesium chloride solution is formed, which has to be treated to recover the chloride component of the original acid for recycling to the leach. The Intec approach described above [14] is to precipitate the magnesium as magnesia, much as the commercial magnesia operations do from seawater 7 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au [24] or lake brines [25]. The Nichromet approach, also described above [11,12,13], is to precipitate the magnesium as carbonate/bicarbonate with carbon dioxide gas, and calcine the product to magnesia.
