In Canada, some process fundamentals have been studied using laterite samples from various tropical locations around the world. The work in Australia has largely been carried out with samples of Young laterite at the laboratories of Metcon, a subsidiary of Ammtec, in Brookvale, a 8 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au suburb of Sydney. The procedure in all cases was to prepare a lixiviant matrix solution comprising a known magnesium chloride concentration, usually at 3.55mb (360 g/L at ambient temperature), taking into consideration the moisture content of the ore. The ore/magnesium chloride slurry was heated to just below the desired temperature, and the first addition of commercial concentrated hydrochloric acid (31.5% HCl) added. Additional crystals of MgCl2.6H2O were then added to maintain the initial magnesium concentration, which is very important to do, since the extent of magnesium leaching is an important parameter. When investigating the effect of acid addition, the acid was added in increments and allowed to react for one hour in a single test for the tropical laterites, but carried out as a series of separate tests with intermediate sampling for the Young laterite. When other parameters were being investigated, the acid was added all at once. ###### **5.1 PROCESS FUNDAMENTALS** ###### **5.1.1 Acid to Ore Ratio** If it is accepted that the single most important criterion for the success of any process, especially one involving feeds with such low head grades as laterites have, is the recovery of nickel (and cobalt), then simply put, sufficient hydrochloric acid has to be added to the laterite slurry to effect acceptable extraction of the nickel and cobalt values contained within the ore. Figure 2 shows the effect of increasing aci

d addition on the extraction of nickel, iron and magnesium from a tropical saprolite ore. This figure suggests that about 30% of the nickel was extracted for very little acid addition or very little iron leaching; occasionally, for some laterites, this figure has been as high as 80%, but the lower figure seen here is much more common. As further acid was added, the extraction of both iron and nickel increased uniformly with about 500 kg/tonne being required to achieve 90% nickel recovery for this particular ore. The behaviour of magnesium, however, was somewhat different to that of the base metals, with its extraction initially decreasing, even with increasing acid addition, before redissolving with continued further acid addition. This behaviour of magnesium has been noted previously [1,2,3] and is discussed more fully later in the paper (section 5.3). ###### **5.1.2 Kinetics of Leaching** The kinetics of leaching at the low acid addition (150 kg/tonne) required by the Jaguar Process [4] are shown in Figure 3. The data show that there was very rapid leaching in the first 15 minutes for nickel, iron and magnesium, and thereafter a very slow increase in nickel extraction corresponding to a decrease in iron extraction. This rapid leaching in concentrated chloride brines is characteristic of all laterites investigated, and provided that sufficient acid has been added, then the reaction (for the base metals, not magnesium) is generally more or less instantaneous, such that when 500-600 kg/tonne is added, ~90% of the base metals leach immediately. Such behaviour has been reported previously [2,3]. Magnesium extraction shows what appears to be the typical initial leaching followed by precipitation and then leaching again, as the iron was presumably neutralized and precipitated, and this behaviour is discussed in more detail later. Figure 2 and Figure 3 demonstrate the general behaviour of all the laterites tested with chloride brines, that the kinetics of leaching for the base metals are very rapid, whereas magnesium behaviour can be quite complex.  It is also demonstrated that increasing acid addition is generally necessary to achieve high metal recovery, because, except in a few cases, it is necessary to break down the matrices of the mineral in order to liberate the nickel. ###### **5.1.3 Temperature Effects** 

Figure 5 below shows the effect of temperature on metal extraction for Jervois Young saprolite. The results suggest little temperature effect on cobalt and manganese extraction, but that there is an optimum around 105°C for nickel (and iron) extraction.  The test at 105°C was conducted at a different time, earlier in the programme, to the others, but the results suggest that the different conditions had little effect on base metal leaching.  The behaviour of magnesium is again of interest.  At the lower percentage solids (10.3%), there is a distinct trend to appreciably increased leaching with increasin

g temperature, which strongly suggests that, as expected (and one of the reasons for its use), the amount magnesium leached is actually tied to the solubility of magnesium chloride at the specific temperature, which continues increasing up to temperatures of about 180°C at atmospheric pressure. If the absolute amount of magnesium leached for the 105°C test (17.3% solids) is prorated to 10.3% solids, then the extraction would have been 57%, again suggesting that the solubility effect was a factor. This value is slightly higher than extrapolation of the curve would suggest because the initial magnesium chloride matrix was lower (360 g/L) in the 105°C test than it was in the others (400 g/L), thus allowing for more magnesium to leach. A logical conclusion from this temperature-solubility-extraction effect is that under continuous operation, where the leach reactors operate at the **terminal** conditions, magnesium 11 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au leaching should be significantly suppressed. This value is the same as that attained at a similar temperature during operation of the Magnola Metallurgy commercial magnesium leach plant in Quebec [26], where asbestos tailings (magnesium silicates) were leached in hot concentrated hydrochloric acid for the recovery of magnesium, and is regarded as being the highest operationally achievable under these conditions. The base metals (Ni, Co, Mn) are not affected in the same manner, because they are significantly below their solubility limits (20-30 g/L) in these brines. The case of ferric iron, however, is somewhat different again. Its solubility in such solutions is very high and somewhat indeterminate [22], being very much a function of the crystalline solid phase with which it is in equilibrium. It is, however, certainly the equivalent of magnesium at leaching temperatures and where goethite or ferrihydrite is the predominant solid phase. ###### **6 IRON PRECIPITATION AND LIXIVIANT REGENERATION** 

As noted earlier in this paper, the common methods proposed (as opposed to actual practice) of dealing with the iron in solution have been either (i) precipitation with a base, usually recycled magnesia from pyrohydrolysis, to form an oxyhydroxide/oxide, primarily hematite, or (ii) solvent extraction followed by pyrohydrolysis of the resultant ferric chloride solution.  In the former case, the magnesium chloride solution generated has to be treated by pyrohydrolysis to recover the hydrochloric acid and regenerate the magnesia, whereas in the latter, the acid is recovered directly.  However, it should be noted that pyrohydrolysis of iron chlorides generally start with ferrous, since it is much easier and more efficient than starting with ferric.  It is only relatively recently that ferric chloride has even been considered as a viable option [29].  Simple calculations for both cases above show that neither scenario can tolerate very much iron (ferrous plus ferric) in solution (certainly <5 g/L) before the process is rendered uneconomic due to the pyrohydrolysis energy demand. 

Thus, the high acid demand, high iron-leaching process described in this paper would seem to be contrary to the above logic, unless there is a different way of handling the iron solutions and regenerating the acid.  Fortunately, there is, but it is beyond the scope of this paper

to go into any discussion at this time; a subsequent publication will present more details on the background of the technique [22], for which patent applications have been filed [30,31], since it is applicable equally to the leaching of polymetallic sulphide ores [32]. 

Very briefly, even though the pregnant leach solutions are highly concentrated, there is still sufficient water to effect the following equilibrium reaction: 

###### 2FeCl3  +  3H2O  ↔  Fe2O3  +  6HCl 

The vapour pressure of HCl over concentrated magnesium chloride is much higher than it is over water, and hence, it is theoretically possible if desired for the HCl to be distilled off and recycled to the leach, thus forcing the above equilibrium to the right hand side of the equation.  This is a very simplistic view of what is a complex series of both simultaneous and sequential reactions, which is currently under detailed investigation at McGill University in Canada.  Highly crystalline, pure hematite has been made by this technique, and preliminary calculations carried out with the commercially available modelling software AspenPlus® indicate that the process should be a low energy consumer.

###### **7 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS** 

A review has been carried out in which the original key concept of the Jaguar Nickel high chloride leaching process, namely simultaneous iron leaching and precipitation, have been shown to be largely incompatible with high metal recovery and low acid consumption.  Consequently, a new approach, wherein as much acid is added as is necessary to achieve maximum metal extraction, has been proposed.  Batch agitation and bottle roll leach tests on the four resource types present in the Jervois Young Laterite deposit in New South Wales using this approach have shown that, even though the head grades are low, high metal recoveries can be attained using a magnesium chloride-hydrochloric acid lixiviant system. 

Concurrently, a low temperature, low energy system is being developed for iron removal as hematite and regeneration of the lixiviant solution.  Preliminary energy and mass balances using AspenPlus® suggest that the process should be economic even with the low head grades experienced at Young.  Jervois is therefore planning to move forward with process development, comprising operating an agitation leach mini pilot plant circuit later in 2006. 

Additionally, preliminary filtration tests, conducted on fresh terminal chloride leach slurries prepared at Metcon Laboratories, by RPA Process Technologies (Filtres Philippe) have indicated high filtration rates (much higher than typical commercial zinc plant jarosites, for example), such that vacuum belt filters can be contemplated for a commercial plant.  This will be a considerable operating and capital cost advantage over the CCD circuit normally required for PAL plants.

The attrition section of the scrubber is specifically designed for high velocity operation in viscous pulp. The LIGHTNIN Attrition Scrubber uses a lower axial flow **_LIGHTNIN ATTRITION_** up-pumping impeller in combination with an upper down-pumping **_LIGHTNIN ATTRITION_** impeller. The **_LIGHTNIN ATTRITION_** impellers are three bladed high solidity selections optimised for D/T and spacing, which ensures minimum by passing and maximum shear between the impeller zones. The high flow and low power characteristics combined with a uniform discharge velocity profile creates a shear zone between the impellers that dramatically exceeds the level of mechanical shear which can be imparted by the use of Rushtons without sacrificing flow and consuming less power. The up-pumping / down-pumping configuration results in a pseudo radial flow pattern, which results form the high impact collision of the impeller discharges. Subsequent fluid modelling has shown that the level of fluid shear exceeds that of mechanical shear at the same applied power level. ###### 1. INTRODUCTION 

###### 1.1. IMPORTANCE OF UNDERSTANDING PAL FEED RHEOLOGY 

A pressure acid leach (PAL) process is used to extract nickel from ore containing predominantly two mineral types, limonite and saprolite.  Typically, ore is blended, screened, crushed, slurried  with hot process water, transported by pipeline and thickened prior to being leached in an autoclave where processing takes place at low pH and elevated temperature and pressure. 

Refining nickel laterites using pressure acid leach technologies requires that the solids concentration of the feed to the autoclave is maximized whilst favourable rheological, or flow, characteristics are maintained to ensure adequate heat transfer and efficient reaction rates.  The solids concentration of the autoclave feed should be maximised in order to minimise the size and cost of the autoclaves and associated unit operations for a given throughput.  When designing the key plant areas upstream of the autoclave, the objective is to balance the desire to maximise the feed concentration without compromising (a) the efficiency of the autoclave and (b) the pumping and thickening efficiency of other plant areas.  As the autoclave feed concentration is increased, the heat transfer efficiency may be compromised due to the formation of slugs, along with an increase in the pumping energy requirements.  The aim for designers and operators is to maximise the feed concentration whilst maintaining favourable rheological properties. 

Although the solids concentration of the autoclave feed is important from a cost and throughput perspective, it is ultimately the rheological characteristics which are crucial for successful design and operation of the feed thickening and handling systems and the autoclave.  For nickel l

aterites, the solids concentration required to achieve the design rheology may vary dramatically depending on the ore mineralogy and the processing conditions. 

Understanding the rheological characteristics of PAL feeds is now a recognised prerequisite to effective system design, operation and risk management.  However, the methods of assessing these rheological characteristics are many and varied and care must be taken to ensure that the data are generated in a manner which is relevant to the proposed application.  Furthermore, testwork programmes must be developed in a way that ensures that all pertinent issues will be identified and, where possible, quantified. Comprehensive and systematic rheological characterisation provides input to allow the appropriate design and optimisation of the key plant areas through manipulation of the ore blend ratio, solids concentration, shear history effects and temperature. 

Since mid 2001, Rheological Consulting Services (RCS) have tested and analysed over 50 nickel laterite ore samples from numerous deposits worldwide and have been engaged to review rheological data generated by nine other testing facilities.  A systematic framework for rheological assessment has been developed (Sofrа 2006) which is presented along with examples to highlight the care which must be taken to ensure that data obtained are relevant to the autoclave feed thickening and handling systems.  The paper is designed to guide the reader through a checklist of rheological questions to ask and issues to address - from sampling to testing protocols, data analysis and informed data application. 

###### 1.2. THE NEED FOR A SYSTEMATIC FRAMEWORK FOR RHEOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT 

The mineralogical composition and physical constitution of nickel laterite ores varies between deposits within deposits and during ‘life of mine’.  Understanding how these variations impact on the ‘processability’ of ores is an essential step in identifying and mitigating project risk and aiding the ongoing sustainable operation of the processing plant. 

In some cases in the past, plants have been designed using minimal rheological data obtained for limited or ‘representative’ samples.  Due to a number of rheology related failures and process difficulties encountered in these projects, it is now understood that this  practice results in excessive risk.  Nickel laterite ores can exhibit significant variations in both the magnitude of rheological parameters and the actual rheological phenomena observed.  Therefore, failure to define and quantify the range of behaviour evident throughout the ore body, may result in the design of feed thickening and handling systems which are unable to meet the autoclave concentration, throughput and/or flow characteristic requirements.  Rheological studies are becoming increasingly detailed and aimed at gaining a comprehensive understanding of the variations in the rheological properties throughout the ore body and the impact of these varia

tions on the successful operation of the plant.

Some nickel laterite slurries possess unique rheological characteristics rarely seen in the minerals industry relating to shear history effects, whilst others possess characteristics commonly observed in mineral suspensions.  As both unique and common behaviour may be evident in one ore body, it is essential that the variations in the deposit are identified and appropriate strategies are employed to ensure that the plant will accommodate the feed presented. 

###### 2. DETERMINING THE EFFECT OF ORE VARIABILITY 

###### 2.1. MINERALOGY AND PARTICLE SIZE DISTRIBUTION 

Where it is known that the ore body contains significant variations in mineralogy, for example limonites and saprolites in a nickel laterite deposit, reconciling mineralogy with the resultant rheological characteristics provides important information for mine planning and ore blending requirements and for determining the expected range of operating conditions for the concentrating plant.  Design of operations relies on an understanding from the outset of the variability expected in rheological properties attributable to the ore type, blended or unblended, being processed and transported. 

Due to changes in mineralogy and effects such as weathering, there can be large variations in the friability and therefore Particle Size Distribution (PSD) throughout the ore body and during the life of mine.  The deviation in PSD must be determined from the outset as particle size dramatically affects the rheology of slurries and pastes and thus the ease of processing and disposal. 

Changes in mineralogy and/or PSD within a deposit can mean an order of magnitude variation in the tailings yield stress (the stress required to initiate flow) at a given solids concentration and can be the difference between a successful and unsuccessful tailings disposal operation.  Figure 1 illustrates the variations in the yield stress profiles of feed samples from one lateritic nickel deposit as a result of changes in mineralogy.  Note that for a yield stress of 200Pa, the solids concentration varies from approximately 42wt% to 56wt%, or alternatively, at a solids concentration of 50wt%, the material properties range from those of a semi-solid i.e. not pumpable with an unmeasurably high yield stress (>1200 Pa), to a yield stress of about 30Pa i.e. easily pumpable with the consistency of pouring cream.  The role of additives such as flocculants is also highlighted, whereby the presence of a flocculant is observed to increase the yield stress of a saprolite-limonite blend.

Those who frequently conduct rheological testwork understand the critical nature of sample preparation and management in order to ensure that the results will accurately reflect the processing conditions. Whether the samples are a result of pilot plant trials or full scale plant operation, at times there may be a delay between sample generation and testing. In the event of this delay, it is important to consider the effects of sample aging and transport. 4 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au Sample aging is particularly important for flocculated samples where the flocculant may degrade over time, samples generated at elevated temperature where cooling may affect the rheology and samples containing clays, where clays may delaminate and swell over time. In these cases, on-site testing is recommended at the time of sample generation and at the process temperature. During transportation to a testing facility both aging and shear history effects may be significant. As the sample is transported it is inevitable that the shear history experienced will differ from plant conditions. Obviously, in the case of shear history dependent materials (where the rheology varies with time of shear as for many nickel laterites) this will result in variations in the measured rheology compared with plant conditions. Settling and particle size segregation is also likely, requiring the sample to be homogenised and resuspended prior to te

sting. Although extensive efforts are made to minimise the effects mentioned, they are sometimes unavoidable and often the only prudent approach is to ensure the data is utilised with awareness of the limitations imposed by sample preparation. ###### 3. SHEAR STRESS VS SHEAR RATE A flow curve, or rheogram shows the shear stress as a function of shear rate and therefore the viscosity as a function of shear rate. Flow curves need to be measured over the anticipated operating range indicated by yield stress profiles and may also need to encompass a range of shear histories (from unsheared to fully sheared). Although these three materials possess the same yield stress, the rheograms clearly show how different the flow characteristics are. The saprolite is best described as a Bingham plastic and is insensitive to shear history whereas the limonite is highly shear thinning and shear history sensitive. The ramifications of insufficient investigation into the flow behaviour could be dramatic. If for example, the design yield stress for autoclave feed was 100 Pa and only the saprolite rheology was known, the pre-autoclave thickener would be operated to produce an underflow at 52wt% solids. Clearly, the autoclave feed preparation system would fail if it was attempted to thicken the limonite to 52wt% solids concentration as the unsheared material would behave as a paste with a yield stress >1200 Pa (solid like and un-pumpable). ROTATIONAL METHODS Rotational rheology testing using methods including vane and couette (cup and bob) are convenient, the apparatus being highly portable and requiring small sample volumes. These methods also provide a low cost alternative to pipeloop tests (section 4.3). If used prudently, rotational methods are accurate, however, there are a number of factors to be considered when applying data obtained using rotational devices. Many testing facilities employ ramped measurements, where the shear stress is measured as the shear rate is progressively increased (or decreased) from one value to the successive value. There are a number of issues associated with this testing approach which need to be considered when testing nickel laterites: 9 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au - Each measurement is dependent on the shear rate and duration of shear of preceding measurements in the sweep. As m

any nickel laterites are sensitive to shear history, this approach results in the material being in a different structural state for each measurement – essentially the same material is not being tested at each shear rate. 

- Particle migration away from the shearing surface may take place over the duration of the test resulting in measurement of a low concentration region not representative of the bulk sample. For smooth bobs rotating in a cup, slip may occur at the bob surface, again resulting in measurement of a low concentration region not representative of the bulk sample. 

- For shear thinning or thixotropic slurries, the reduction in the viscosity over the duration of the test may result in particle settling and the formation of a concentration gradient along the length of the shearing surface. 

- Evaporation at high temperature may be significant, thereby increasing the concentration of the sample being tested over the duration of a test.  As most nickel laterites are processed at elevated temperature and the yield stress and viscosity are temperature dependent, it is important that rheology testing is conducted at the process temperature. 

For the majority of slurries and pastes, ramped measurements are inappropriate and a superior approach is to conduct individual measurements at successive shear rates with minimal, gentle homogenisation of the sample between measurements. 

A good way to check the validity of flow data from rotational testing (or any testing for that matter) is to compare the low shear rate data with an independently measured vane yield stress.  If the low shear rate data do not coincide with the yield stress this indicates that one or more of the above factors may be prevalent. 

###### 4.3. ‘PIPE’ METHODS 

A tubular geometry is often preferred given the similarity with pipeline flow. Examples include capillary (small tube) rheometry and pipeloop tests.  For capillary testing care must be taken to eliminate wall and end effects by ensuring that the tube length and diameter are appropriate for the PSD of the sample.  In order to minimise the possibility of wall and end effects, both L/D (tube length/ diameter) and D/d50 should be greater than about 60 where the d50 is the median particle size of the suspended particles. 

Pipeloop testing is often performed to verify simpler rheological testing e.g. rotational methods, and to indicate the parameters such as settling velocities in the presence of shear.  One of the disadvantages with pipeloop tests is that the sample is continually recirculated, making determination of shear history effects difficult.  Pipeloop tests are rarely conducted as part of an initial rheological characterisation programme as they are time consuming, expensive and large sample sizes are required.

No matter how ‘good’ the rheological data, it is imperative that the end-user ensure that rheological information is applied appropriately.  One of the fi

rst things to consider is whether the data are relative or absolute. Relative data, for example slump heights for a particular material or flow data obtained for a different shear history condition to that of the process, can be useful in it’s own right, but the user must be aware that the information may be best for ranking, comparative or ‘indication of change’ purposes rather than direct design input. ###### 5.1. AUTOMATED INSTRUMENT ANALYSES Many commercial rheometer software packages use models which are unsuitable for yield stress fluids and employ a Newtonian analysis for materials which are clearly non-Newtonian. A competent testing facility will be aware of this and analyse the raw instrument readings appropriately rather than relying on inappropriate automated analyses. ###### 5.2. RHEOLOGICAL MODELS . Flow data, or shear stress (τ) as a function of shear rate (γ ) are often presented in the form of a rheological model. The most commonly used models are the Bingham and Herschel-Bulkley models, shown in Equations 1 and 2 respectively. 10 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au The Bingham Model has historically been used for prediction of pipeline transport requirements, where the shear rates of interest are of the order of 10 to 100s-1 . For pipeline start-up conditions, rake drive requirements and vessel agitation, the shear rates of interest are much lower (zero for pipeline start-up conditions and rake drive requirements and 5 to 15s-1 for agitation), so the Bingham parameters are largely unsuitable. Still, metallurgical problems are among the main causes leading to disappointing project outcome. The most serious difficulties often arise in the case of projects involving difficult ores, generally requiring novel and/or complex flowsheets. The paper discusses pilot plant practices proven to be effective in producing metallurgical test data of sufficient reliability to effectively minimise metallurgical project risks. The causes and remedies of poor metallurgical performance at the pilot plant level are also discussed. Broader technical management issues covered include design, construction and operation of complex hydrometallurgical pilot plants. Particular emphasis is placed on pilot plant operations with respect to their preparation, management, design, operation and most importantly, overlooked metallurgical issues. Piloting experiences discussed include flowsheets treating polymetallic feed samples containi

###### 1. INTRODUCTION – THE BIG PICTURE 

Current and predicted metals prices seem to confirm a sustainable upturn in the mining business. This (long overdue) positive trend inevitably leads to increased project activity.  When new projects come on line there is an increased chance that some of these new plants encounter problems during commissioning, which in turn can have quite a negative effect on the industry. There are opinions whereby metallurgical risk is among the leading causes of the failure of mining projects - some believe in fact, and with good justification, that after resource risk, metallurgical risks account for most of the failures of mining projects [1].  This situation does not appear to be changing for the good, in spite of the fact that metallurgy should be more “controllable” compared to other areas of lower risk, such as financing, environmental, political, market, etc.  The chances for lowering metallurgical risk could in fact be diminishing as the global workload is increasing while the supply of a qualified workforce remains relatively unchanged for the short to medium term.  This may well be the legacy of the extended period of weak metal markets and thus characterised by a lack of interest in the extractive metallurgical profession.  The root causes leading to metallurgical failures, particularly with respect to their effect on ramp-up times, have been discussed [2, 3].  The purpose of this paper is to focus on the pilot scale metallurgical testing and its role in preventing metallurgical failure.  Particular emphasis is placed on pilot plant operations with respect to their preparation, management, design, operation and overlooked metallurgical issues.  The underlying logic of piloting is disarmingly simple – a pilot plant contains most of the critical attributes of a commercial plant that allow for the evaluation of the metallurgical response of typical feed samples.  A pilot plant is designed and built having the clear objective of trouble-free commissioning and rapid ramp-up to designed tonnage throughput and metallurgical performance.  Reaching these objectives generally tends to indicate the existence of a positive metallurgical environment whereby fatal operating errors are unlikely.  A modern continuous pilot plant allows for cost-effective operation while maximizing the quantity and quality of the data produced.  Good operation does not necessarily preclude the existence of process flaws – the data produced will however flag these problems. 

Producing data requires that the pilot plant operation starts-up and operates as planned.  Key to achieving this is detailed preparation, as will be discussed below.  This paper highlights the importance of establishing the flowsheet design during the laboratory phase preceding the pilot plant, in order to maximise its chances of success.

Limitations of the pilot plants include: 

- The data produced by the pilot plant will tend to reflect the behaviour of the samples tested, hence the need of sample variability testing for those projects with predicted long term mineralogically diverse deposits; 

- Existence of unit operations that can not be commonly replicated in a manner that allows for generation of scale-up data – examples include oxygen mass transfer, especially at atmospheric pressure, pressure autoclaving, heat losses/balancing, long distance pipeloop operation, etc.; 

- The long term behaviour of certain equipment (pumps, compressors, drives, sensors, etc.) may not be fully ascertained through a pilot plant exercise, because pilot plants are never operated for long enough; 

- Failure of materials of construction is sometimes difficult to predict based on pilot plant operations.  Examples include mechanical erosion (flash vessels, choke valves), stress corrosion cracking, certain solvent extraction related scaling, anode damage. 

- Replication of process control strategies is often difficult due to less automation encountered in the pilot pant, which in turn is limited by the low flowrates. 

The Ultimate Limitation 

The ultimate limitation of a pilot plant is that it can not be used efficiently and cost effectively for process flowsheet optimization testing.  This limitation is very important.  In fact, a pilot plant is the most expensive process optimization.  Accordingly, attempting to carry out process optimization during the pilot plant operation will significantly increase the project risk. This does not preclude normal operational flexibility that a well-designed pilot plant is expected to allow for. Indeed, this is the strength of pilot operations where allowances for sample variability testing, adjustment of certain parameters within pre-planned limits, necessary corrections in recycle stream flowrates (as a result of changing conditions) are included as part of the program.  In practice this means that the design, sizing and construction of the equipment, piping and peripherals should permit for adjusting of the residence time in the various circuits, as required by each individual metallurgical sample tested. 

The limitations of a given pilot plant should be analysed with respect to its main goal.  A “proof of concept” pilot plant for example should provide more flexibility compared to a “feasibility stage” pilot plant.  On the other hand, flexibility should be realistically limite

d such that real life conditions are maintained as close as possible. 

###### 3. RAMP-UP, DURATION, EXPECTATIONS 

The differences, similarities and limitations listed above clearly suggest that a pilot plant can be compared to a commercial plant in its very early commissioning and ramp up stages.  But, at the same time, they highlight the main difference between the pilot plant and the commercial plant, whereby a pilot plant must reach its nominal throughput within hours, versus ramp up times of months or years in a commercial plant.  The first important decision regarding the planning of the pilot plant refers to its intended duration, which in turn is determined by generally conflicting considerations, for example metallurgical versus promotional, financial and others.  The average duration of the modern hydrometallurgical pilot plant has decreased in recent years to about four weeks, which includes about two to three weeks of fully integrated steady-state operation.  By comparison, the late nineties pilot plant campaigns were up to three months in duration, such as

###### 4. MANAGING CHANGE 

The need for managing changes during a major metallurgical program is not new, but it has become more stringent recently because of the realities of modern pilot plants.  Managing change begins from the inception of the pilot plant and it involves key decision making and operating people assigned to the project.  In a sense, it can be stated that changes tend to become the “backbone” of the piloting business, a very unique common component that can be singled out in every pilot project. 

This paper will focus on objective changes needed to successfully mitigate the metallurgical risks, with emphasis on flowsheet development: 

The main elements of the positive change-management process in the case of flowsheet

changes include: 

- Detailed flowsheet analyses, with emphasis on its “pilotability”. 

- Analysis of the implications of the changes regarding generally overlooked aspects that affect operability.  These may include liquid-solid separation, rheology, effect of recycle, effect on integrating downstream unit operations on residence and hold-up times; issues related to corrosion. 

- Carrying out overall risk to reward ratio analysis, based on a comprehensive supporting bench scale testwork program.  This step is the most difficult to put into practice. However, it is generally the only one that provides certainty and a positive outcome, should the results warrant it. 

An example of positive management is provided below, and it is inspired from the realities of the routine preparations involved in a pilot plant.  The underlying philosophy is that a successful pilot plant relies on a well established flowsheet, which does not require further changes during the operation. This allows for testing the response of several feed samples.  This process may require a significant number of revisions of the original flowsheet.  The revisions can be done generally based on extensive bench scale testwork, in conjunction with pre-pilot runs.  The end result is a “pilotable” flowsheet, characterised first and foremost by operability.

###### 5. EXAMPLE – PRESSURE OXIDATION AUTOCLAVE – DISCHARGE OPTIONS 

###### Scenario 

This example describes certain details related to the preparation (i.e. planning and designing) of a pilot plant in which sulphidic concentrates were oxidized by oxygen in a continuous autoclave. SGS Minerals Services carried out this exercise as part of an in-house development program focussing on generic pilot plant flowsheet development and planning.  The goal of the study was to determine the best available autoclave discharge treatment option that would allow for smooth operation of the downstream pilot plant.  The feed sample consisted of a polymetallic sulphide concentrate containing 29% S, 24% (Cu+Ni+Co) and 11 g/t Au. 

The discussion provided in this particular section is limited to factors that influence the operability of the continuous pressure oxidation (POX) in a pilot autoclave, with specific focus on discharge treatment options.  The continuous POX autoclaving process was followed by liquid-solid separation in conjunction with partial neutralization to pH ~ 2, using limestone slurry.  Whilst quite commonly applied, this generic sequence of unit operations is still sufficiently complex to create problems during pilot plant operation, if not prepared with attention to certain details, as discussed below. 

###### Risks 

<u>POX parameters scale up</u> - from bench (“Parr”) test to continuous operation – from a pure process chemistry point of view, the optimisation of POX leaching parameters is generally a routine bench scale exercise and produces straightforward results.  Scale-up pro

blems are quite rare and they can be generally addressed successfully by carrying out a few pre-pilot plant continuous POX runs.  Continuous operation allows for better understanding of the POX process, allows for "fine-tuning" of parameters such as oxygen flowrate, pressure and off-gas content. Agitator rotation speed ("RPM regime") and feed solids density for autothermal operations are also important parameters that can be determined / confirmed relatively easily during the pre-pilot runs.   The process chemistry is often somewhat different in the continuous autoclave compared to batch POX, particularly related to oxidation of iron sulphides and the type of iron hydrolysis compounds formed.  Reaction kinetics can also be subtly different, and because of the impact on downstream equipment sizing, optimum throughput rate in the autoclave needs to be confirmed in short pre-pilot plant runs.  Other issues that can be looked at during the pre-pilot plant include corrosion related issues, analytical sampling and sample processing, data collection and reduction, with emphasis on mass balance and accountability.  Corrosion testing may not always be accommodated within the fully integrated pilot plant because of issues relating to the stability of dissolved species and the risk of contamination by the eventual corrosion products. 

<u>Feed issues – although often a simple issue, feed characterisation is critical to the continuous</u> POX process.  Severe problems can arise for example if the pilot plant feed is different from the bench scale feed.  Feed inconsistency quite frequently occurs in commercial operations.  The implications can be quite grave because feed composition affects the process chemistry, which in turn affects the downstream unit operations.  Avoiding some of the feed related issues can also be successfully addressed during the pre-pilot continuous runs.  On the other hand, feed variability testing can be a critical aim of the pilot plant operation requiring constant attention throughout its duration. 

<u>Operability – autoclave feed and control issues generally take precedence during the preparation</u> stage of the pilot plant, and pre-pilot runs allow for detailed “debugging” of any problems that may arise. 

The most significant overlooked aspect however relates to the handling of the autoclave discharge slurry from the perspective of liquid-solid separation and rheology (“LSR”), along with

###### Overview of the continuous pre-pilot POX runs results 

Bench scale testwork determined several POX conditions from which a set of three was selected for further confirmation/optimisation through continuous autoclave pre-pilot runs.  The objective of the pre-pilot runs was to investigate the conditions that would ensure autothermal operation, acceptable metal extractions and downstream operability.  The runs were carried out on a representative composite feed sample, with allowance for about 20 hours of steady state operating time to test each set of parameters.  Sample variability was briefly tested towards the end of the exercise, for about 6 hours operating time each. 

The continuous run results indicated that maximum Cu/Ni/Co extractions of about 95% each could be achieved under the following conditions: feed grind size K80 ~ 70 microns, temperature - 210ºC, 90 minutes residence time.   Feed solids density of ~12% wt. was needed to ensure autothermal conditions for 210ºC operating temperature.  Lowering the feed solids density below ~12% wt. caused a drop of about 4ºC per each percent solids decrease. 

The pre-pilot POX autoclaving was carried out with particular attention to maximising extractions (Table 1) while minimising the ratio between the basic iron sulphate (BFS) and hematite formed during the process.  Hematite is generally stable at higher temperatures (>200ºC) and relatively low acidity (<30 g/L at 200ºC in this case).  At a certain temperature, the main factor determining the BFS/hematite ratio is the free acidity produced by oxidation of the sulphur, which in turn is determined by its availability (in the feed), as well as its degree of oxidation during the POX process as to allow for autothermal conditions.  In addition, the iron and free acid contained in the recycle solution streams could also ultimately become a potential source of BFS.  Avoiding BFS formation is important for several reasons, including handleability of the discharge slurry, environmental stability of the tailings and optimum cyanidation process chemistry, in case of a downstream gold plant.

###### Scenario 1 – Hot curing of the POX discharge Option A 

Hot curing is a variation of Option A which allows for the decomposition of the basic iron sulphate (BFS) by its reaction with sulphuric acid at 90ºC and atmospheric pressure.  The reaction equation is depicted below: 

2Fe(OH)SO4 + H2SO4 Fe2(SO4)3 + 2H2O 

Practically, this reaction is the reverse of the BFS formation reaction, which takes place at 200ºC and under oxygen pressure.  The hot curing reaction is reasonably fast (several hours) at 90ºC, and consumes acid while bringing iron into solution as ferric sulphate.  Hot curing is considered sometimes as an option in the case of certain gold and occasionally, PGM projects. 

###### <u>Advantages of this route include:</u> 

- The sulphuric acid would be converted into ferric sulphate; 

- The weight of the residue would decrease thus increasing the gold grade in the CIL feed, compared to Option B; 

- The underflow would display higher solids densities (due to less BFS), requiring fewer CCD stages and less wash water; 

- The main advantage of hot curing is for applications in which the autoclave solids are processed for gold recovery.  If the solids contain BFS when proceeding to a gold cyanidation circuit, all of the acid in the solids (as BFS) must be consumed by lime (which is expensive) before the pH of the slurry will stabilize >pH 10.  After hot curing and CCD however, when the BFS has been converted to ferric sulphate, the acidity associated with the iron compounds can all be neutralized with limestone which is usually at least 10 times cheaper than lime. 

###### <u>Possible disadvantages include:</u> 

- An additional circuit needed; 

- Heating and mixing costs; 

- Need for closed tanks to contain/limit evaporation; 

- Silver recovery usually decreases, due to stable silver jarosite formation during hot curing 

Analogous to considerations discussed in the previous section, the decision would require preparatory metallurgical testwork as part of the pre-pilot program, because the hot curing feed sample must be fresh.  Conversely, sudden implementation could negatively affect the process. Past pilot plants produced good results when employing hot curing.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Titanium’s superior corrosion resistance is ideal for many  process applications (Ref 1).  Process industries choose titanium as the material of construction for piping, tanks, pressure vessels, columns, autoclaves, and heat exchangers.   When pressures and/or temperatures and size demand very thick plate, the titanium equipment can become considerably more expensive than units constructed  from lower cost, lower performance materials.   Titanium clad steel offers a reliable, cost effective alternative, providing durable titanium lined equipment which is lower cost than many less reliable alternatives.  Titanium clad steel pressure vessels, constructed using explosion welded clad plates, have been in service since the 1960’s.  Over this period, the requirements for vessel size, operating

###### **TYPICAL EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS** 

The demand for titanium clad is dominated by equipment for manufacture of two highly different products, polyester and nickel.  Both have the common need for large, high pressure, high temperature, corrosion resistant equipment.  Differences in corrosion and erosion conditions drive significant differences in the equipment design and construction. 

The largest single application of titanium clad equipment has been in construction of reactors, crystallizer pressure vessels,  and columns for manufacture of Purified Terephthalic Acid (PTA).   PTA is a polymer intermediate used in manufacture of polyester based products, ranging from fibers to PET food containers.  As the world demand for polyester based products has continually grown over recent decades, the demand for titanium clad manufacturing equipment has followed suit.  In parallel, the continuing efforts to reduce product costs have driven the process designers to ever increasing plant capacities.  The largest and heaviest titanium clad equipment in a modern PTA plant are the reactor, Figure 1, and the dehydration tower Figure 2.   Operating conditions are typically 200 to 220°C and 20 to 22 bar.   Titanium is totally impervious to corrosive attack in this environment. Titanium’s selection assures long term, low maintenance performance while also assuring product purity.  With the exception of areas around mechanical connections, such as nozzle and flange faces, crevice corrosion is not a concern.  Unalloyed titanium, ASTM B265 Grade 1, is the al

###### **VESSEL CONSTRUCTION DESIGN ISSUES** 

Titanium clad equipment requires unique fabrication and welding processes when contrasted to stainless steel and nickel alloy clad equipment.  When fabricating the latter, clad is restored over the steel joints using weld overlay processes.  Due to formation  of brittle Ti-Fe intermetallics, this is not possible with titanium-steel clad.  Traditionally the clad restoration in titanium clad fabrication has been achieved using batten straps (Ref 2) which are placed on top of the cladding and welded at the edges with fillet welds.  Figure 4 shows a cross section of a traditional batten strap weld, in case of 8 mm cladding. 

When the titanium cladding layer is relatively thin, such as in the PTA equipment, this technology has an excellent production and performance record. It is difficult to inspect the welds.  The stresses in the welds can be high due to differential thermal expansion issues. The batten strap stands proud inside the vessel presenting concerns with location of internals and complicating issues when erosion is a concern.

ABSTRACT The price of nickel has recently been variable and relatively high. Because it represents a significant proportion of the costs of the materials used for making stainless steel, this has created interest in trying to reduce the nickel content. This paper explains the various contributions which nickel makes to the properties of stainless steels, in particular: formability, weldability, toughness, corrosion resistance, lustre and high temperature properties. Three lower-nickel stainless steel types are discussed: ferritic, duplex and 200-series (as well as proprietary grades of this type). The general characteristics of these three types are described, as well as typical niche market applications for each. It is concluded that every grade of stainless steel has its own properties and characteristics and that it is most important for the specifier to have access to reliable data, including performance histories and case studies, on which to make rational materials decisions. ###### 1.1. THE METALLURGY ###### What is stainless steel? Stainless steel is the name given to a group of corrosion resistant and high temperature steels. Their remarkable resistance to corrosion is due to a chromium-rich oxide film which forms on the surface. When ordinary carbon steel is exposed to rain water, for example, it corrodes forming a brown iron oxide, commonly called rust, on the surface. This is not protective and eventually the entire piece of steel will corrode and be converted to rust. But when enough chromium (more than about 10.5%) is added to ordinary steel, the oxide which forms on the surface is quite different – it is very thin, virtually invisible and protective in a wide range of corrosive media. When we look at a piece of stainless steel, we look straight through this very thin protective oxide film and see the bright, shiny surface underneath. This is what we call stainless steel and there are several different types, a

nd many different grades. Chromium is the basic building block of the stainless steels – without it, stainless steel cannot be produced. It is chromium which provides the basic corrosion resistance of the stainless steels – the higher the level of chromium, the better the corrosion resistance. Six of the most important properties which are improved by the addition of nickel are formability, weldability, toughness, corrosion resistance, lustre and high temperature properties and each of these are discussed below. ###### 1. Formability The dominant metallurgical effect of nickel is that it changes the crystal structure of the steel. The crystal structure of carbon steel at room temperature, such as the steel used in a filing cabinet or the plates of a ship’s hull, is called ferrite. It is a body centred cubic (BCC) structure, with one iron (Fe) atom at each corner of a cube and one iron atom in the centre of the body of the cube – see Figure 2. This crystal unit is very small and there are many billions of such crystal units in each cubic millimetre of metal. When chromium (Cr) is added, the chromium atoms replace some of the iron atoms in the crystal but the crystal structure does not change. That is why these simple Fe-Cr grades are referred to as the ferritic stainless steels. 3 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au Ferrite Austenite

Figure 2.  Crystal structures in steel 

The reason why the BCC crystal structure does not change when chromium is added to form stainless steel is because chromium is a ferrite former – it favours the formation of a ferrite structure.  Molybdenum (Mo), which is added to stainless steels such as Type 316 to improve corrosion resistance, is also a ferrite former. 

When nickel is added to stainless steel, it changes the crystal structure from BCC to face centred cubic (FCC) – there is still one atom at each corner of a cube but now, instead of one atom in the centre of the body, there is one atom in the middle of each face.  This structure is called austenite and this is the structure of the austenitic stainless steels, such as the very popular 300-series Types 304 and 316. 

What is the importance of forming austenite, the FCC crystal structure? – because it provides the metal with very good formability.  There are a few other metals which also have this FCC crystal structure, such as aluminium, copper and nickel.  Like austenitic stainless steels, they also have very good forming characteristics.  This excellent formability distinguishes the austenitic grades from the other types of stainless steels. 



Figure 3.  Type 304 stainless steel kitchen sink.  Manufacture of such a shape is a very difficult deep drawing operation and illustrates the excellent formability of the austenite crystal structure created by the addition of nickel. 

###### 2. Weldability 

The austenitic stainless steels also have better weldability than the other stainless steel types. The next most common type of stainless steels are the ferritic grades but these are more susceptible to the effects of impurities and to grain growth during welding, giving poor bend and impact properties.  Steps can be taken to minimise these shortcomings, through control of composition/metallurgy and by very accurate control of welding, such as by using robotic welding processes.  But the inherently better weldability of austenite means that Types 304 and 316 have found good acceptance in fabrication shops worldwide for many decades.

Figure 4. Fabricating a Type 304 stainless steel rotary wine fermenter.  Types 304 and 316 stainless steel are the standard materials for quality wine tanks and associated winery equipment. 

###### 3. Toughness 

The toughness of a material is its ability to absorb energy without breaking.  Domestic glass, for example, may be very strong but even a small amount of impact energy (such as hitting it with a fork or spoon) can shatter it – it has relatively low toughness. 

Metals in general have good toughness, particularly at room temperature and above. However, as the temperature drops below freezing point, the toughness of some metals reduces greatly.  The ferrite crystal structure shows a rapid reduction in toughness with reducing temperature so these materials are never used at low te

mperatures.  On the other hand, austenite has excellent toughness at all temperatures.  So, the materials which are chosen for cryogenic service have an austenitic crystal structure – such as Type 304 stainless steel or aluminium. 

###### 4. Corrosion resistance 

- Reduced rate of propagation of pitting and crevice corrosion 

Studies show that most corrosion of stainless steel is caused by chlorides (wet salt) and is in the form of localised corrosion, such as pitting and crevice corrosion.  Chlorides are present in many environments, the most obvious being seawater and marine atmospheres.  Chlorides are very corrosive and an indication of the resistance of a stainless steel to the initiation of corrosion by chlorides is given by the Pitting Resistance Equivalent, PRE: 

###### PRE = Cr% + 3.3Mo% + 16N% 

It can be seen from this simple formula that, in addition to chromium (Cr), both molybdenum (Mo) and nitrogen (N) have a very beneficial effect in providing stainless steel with resistance to the initiation of corrosion in aggressive chloride environments.

The Hibernia oil production platform, located 300 km off Newfoundland, Canada, contains 2,400 tonnes of such alloys, including about 1,000 tonnes of Type 316 stainless steel for cable trays, weather cladding, blast walls and HVAC ducting. 

Nickel is not included in the PRE equation since it does not have a significant effect on improving the resistance of stainless steels to the <u>initiation of pitting and crevice</u> corrosion in chloride environments.  However, nickel does reduce the rate of <u>propagation of pits and crevice corrosion, as shown in Figure 6.</u> 



Figure 6.  Beneficial effect of nickel on the propagation rate of pitting and crevice corrosion in stainless steel. (International Stainless Steel Forum) 

- Resistance to reducing environments 

Chromium provides stainless steels with resistance to oxidising environments such as oxidising chemicals (like nitric acid) and oxidising atmospheres (like high temperature air inside a furnace).  Nickel is complementary to chromium – it provides resistance to reducing environments such as reducing chemicals (like sulphuric acid) and reducing atmospheres (like hydrocarbon gases at high temperature in petrochemical plants). 

###### 5. Lustre 

It is chromium which gives stainless steel its “stainless” characteristics and appearance but the colour and lustre of stainless steels does vary somewhat between the different types and grades.  It is difficult to be totally objective about aesthetic aspects such as these but nickelcontaining stainless steels are generally looked upon favourably with regard to colour and lustre.  This is particularly the case when they are compared with the Cr-Mn-N (200-series type) stainless steels which appear to be darker in colour with lower lustre.

###### 6. High temperature properties 

This paper is primarily concerned with aqueous corrosion resistance.  However, it should be mentioned that the addition of nickel to stainless steels also results in a significant improvement in high temperature properties, particularly strength, metallurgical stability and stability of the protective surface oxide scale.  Evidence of the importance of nickel in this regard is given by the fact that, when a stainless steel is not adequate, the next step to improved high temperature performance is normally to use a high-nickel alloy. 

###### Other ways of forming austenite in stainless steel 

From the characteristics listed above, it is apparent that one of the main reasons for adding nickel to stainless steel is to form the austenite crystal structure, thereby improving properties such as formability, weldability and toughness.  Because nickel forms austenite, it is called an austenite former.  However, it is not the only element with this property.  Common austenite formers are:

|C|Carbon|

The relative importance of these elements in forming austenite is of interest to people who wish to predict the crystal structure which will form in stainless steel, such as after welding. Various formulae have been developed to calculate a “Nickel Equivalent” and used in well known charts such as the Schaeffler, DeLong and WRC 1992 diagrams.  The multipliers vary somewhat but the following formula gives some indication of the relative importance of these austenite formers: 

###### Nickel Equivalent = Ni% + 30C% + 30N% + 0.5Mn% +0.25Cu% 

As can be seen from this equation, carbon I is a strong austenite former but it cannot be added to corrosion resistant stainless steels since it can give problems with sensitisation and subsequent intergranular corrosion after welding.  Nitrogen (N) also has a strong austenitising effect but it is a gas and only limited amounts can be added to stainless steel without creating porosity problems.  There are also issues associated with the addition of manganese (Mn) and copper (Cu), ranging from reduced refractory life during steelmaking to welding problems, and scrap contamination is a particular concern which is discussed later.

###### 2. THE OPTIONS 

Having covered the basic metallurgy involved in forming the various types of stainless steels which are relevant to this discussion, it is now possible to focus on the alternatives which are available if the objective is to replace established higher nickel grades of stainless steel with lower nickel grades.  These are: 

- Do not add any nickel and allow the ferrite structure to form. 

- Add only about half the amount of nickel which would be required to form an austenitic stainless steel and make a duplex stainless steel. 

- Replace some or all of the nickel with other austenite formers, such as manganese, nitrogen and copper, to form either a true 200-series grade or a proprietary grade of this type. 

Set out below are examples of where these various alternatives have been used. 

###### A. Ferritic stainless steels 

Ferritic grades such as Types 409 and 430 have been available for many years and their characteristics are well known.  They have become firmly established in certain niche markets. 

Type 409, for instance, is commonly specified for automotive exhaust systems since it has adequate corrosion resistance for an under-body application, has sufficient formability and weldability, particularly given that fabrication is tightly controlled through the use of automated processes, and it has relatively low cost.  However, it should be noted that aus

tenitic stainless steel exhaust systems are commonly used for prestige cars.

In some cases, ferritic and austenitic stainless steels compete for the same application – kitchen sinks, for instance.  In developed countries, Type 304 is the standard grade for this application but in some developing countries Type 430 is used instead.  The ferritic grade allows the product to be produced more cheaply but its inherently lower formability means that the bowl of the sink is not as deep and the sides are not as vertical. 

In some situations, a ferritic stainless steel is technically necessary – stainless steel refrigerator bodies are an example.  Type 304 is most commonly used for the bulk of the body but where the magnetic door seals of the refrigerator contact the body, ferritic Type 430 is used since it is magnetic and ensures a leak tight seal, whereas austenitic materials are not magnetic. 

More recently, a number of proprietary grades of high-Cr, Mo-containing ferritic stainless steels such as 22Cr-1Mo have been developed for the roofing and siding of buildings.  A ferritic grade has the advantage that it has a lower coefficient of thermal expansion and so moves less as sunshine heats and cools the structure.  But this advantage must be considered against the lower formability and weldability of such materials compared with an austenitic grade. 

###### B. Duplex stainless steels 

The nickel content of the duplex grades is lower than for corresponding austenitic grades but their price is often not as low as would be expected from the composition, because these grades are more difficult, and hence more expensive, to manufacture.  Edge cracking during rolling, for instance, can significantly reduce yields. 

However, they have two characteristics which have made them very valuable for certain applications: 

- Strength.  The yield strength of annealed 2205, for instance, is about twice that of annealed Types 304 and 316 stainless steel.  This has led to their use in applications such as glass curtain wall support structures and footbridges.  Duplex 2205 is also the preferred material for constructing seagoing chemical tankers where its combination of strength and general corrosion resistance are very attractive. 



Figure 8.  Duplex 2205 stainless steel has become a standard material for the tanks of marine chemical tankers. 

- Resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking (SCC).  This is a type of cracking which can affect austenitic stainless steels, in particular, when they are in contact with hot waters containing dissolved chloride salts.  The ferritic stainless steels are relatively immune to the problem but are not widely used because of welding problems, although Type 444 (18Cr, 2Mo) has found applicatio

n for hot water tanks in some cases, particularly where automated welding is used.  The duplex grades have better weldability and adequate resistance to chloride SCC and have found wide application in industries such as pulp and paper, chemical and petrochemical.

In most cases, the lower nickel content of the duplex stainless steels is incidental – it is a result of the fact that only 50% of the structure should be austenite and hence a lower level of austenite formers should be added.  But grades such as the recently developed 2101 have such a low nickel content that they attract interest specifically because of this. 

###### C. 200-series and other Cr-Mn-N (-Cu) stainless steels 

Cr-Mn-N alloys have been available for many decades and have found a number of niche applications because of two properties: 

- High strength.  In the preceding discussion, nitrogen has been referred to as an austenite former.  But it also increases the strength of stainless steel very significantly so Cr-Mn-N grades can be developed with relatively high strength.  This has led to their use for drive shafts, pump shafts, clamps for holding street signs onto posts and municipal lamp poles.  When used in strip form, these grades are commonly strengthened further by cold work, i.e. by rolling without a subsequent anneal.  Cold working is also commonly used to strengthen the 300-series stainless steels, such as when Type 316 is used to manufacture bolts or when it is used as wire to support yacht masts. 

- Lack of magnetism.  The austenite crystal structure in stainless steel is not magnetic so a grade such as Type 304 can easily be distinguished from a ferritic grade such as Type 430 with a simple magnet.  Type 304 has a reputation worldwide as “quality stainless steel” and, in some countries such as India; this has developed into a belief among domestic consumers that non-magnetic stainless steel is “quality stainless steel”. Magnetic stainless steel, such as a ferritic grade, is considered to be of inferior quality. 

   - Because of this belief, and in order to avoid the cost of nickel, proprietary Cr-Mn-N (-Cu) grades were developed in India for sale to housewives, who would check the “quality” with a magnet.  The main applications have been domestic kitchen utensils – pots, pans, spoons, ladles etc 

It has become a major issue that Cr-Mn-N (-Cu) alloys are not distinguishable from Type 304 without sophisticated analysis and this has led to the widespread misuse of these cheaper grades, particularly over the last couple of years.  In some cases they have been sold as Type 304, or become mixed up with Type 304, and they have been used in applications for which they are not suited, resulting in numerous corrosion failures.  Widespread use of these grades will also pose problems for the recycling industry as they cannot easily be distinguished from Type 304.  Either scrap collectors and traders will have to invest in mu

ch more thorough, and more costly, quality checks or problems will become evident in the 300series scrap circuit, due to unacceptable contamination with manganese and copper. As ease of recycling is seen as one of the major virtues of stainless steels, developments that make recycling more difficult are not helpful. ###### 3. CONCLUSION “There are no bad stainless steels – only badly selected ones” Each type and grade of stainless steel has its own set of characteristics. For some applications, a characteristic may be positive while in other applications it may be negative – high strength, for instance, is beneficial in a structural application but generally makes forming operations more difficult. Each of these characteristics must be taken into account when selecting a stainless steel for a particular use. In order to make rational decisions regarding grade selection, it is essential that reliable data are available – composition, mechanical properties and corrosion resistance under all relevant circumstances. It is also highly desirable that there is an extensive history which can be accessed setting out performance and case studies in similar applications. Before specifying any stainless steel, users should ensure that they have access to all such information. Lower-nickel alternatives such as ferritic, duplex and Cr-Mn-N (-Cu) alloys of various types may be appropriate for various niche applications but it is far from coincidental that the vast majority of stainless steels in use around the world today are nickel containing 300-series austenitic Types 304 and 316. This is because they have a highly desirable combination of properties, are readily available and there is extensive knowledge about their field performance which makes them predictable and low-risk. 11 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au Ultimately, it is the “cost – performance” balance which must be considered when selecting a material for any practical application. The desire to reduce the nickel content of a stainless steel generally arises from a wish to reduce initial purchase cost but, in many cases, this can simultaneously result in a reduction in performance. So any substitution of this type should be made with access to all relevant data and with a complete understanding of the long term cost and performance implications. Otherwise, a less expensive material can easily prove to be a more expensive choice. 12 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au Using

Are there benefits in valve design by using Hydraulic Actuation? For Isolation Valves the lighter more balanced weight of a Hydraulic Actuator reduces the structural requirements of the actuator mounting bracket, reducing costs. It also reduces the tendency for the unbalanced Pneumatic Actuator to pull the stem to one side which can impact valve life. We have spent most of this presentation discussing Isolation Valves. However Hydraulic Actuation can have significant benefits when used on control valves. The stiffer operation offered by Hydraulics allows for much improved control for instance. In addition, due to the non compressible nature of Hydraulics, there is significantly less chance of the ceramic surfaces for the autoclave level control valves coming together resulting in trim damage. This allows for the confident use of a Tight Shut Off design where the ceramics are brought together with a predetermined seating pressure, without the danger of the ‘bath plug effect’ smashing the ceramic surfaces together. 16 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ### ~~Hydraulics for Choke ValvesHydraulics for Choke Valves~~ Here we can see a Tight Shut Off, Ceramic Lined Control Valve. This is a flow over design so as the surfaces come closer together there is a tendency for the ‘Bath Plug Effect’ to hammer the surfaces together. By using Hydraulic Actuation this does not happen and in addition a predetermined seating pressure can be set to operate once the surfaces are brought together. The great benefit of this approach is a plant can close the level control valve before the autoclave isolation valves, thereby reducing the differential pressure on the valves to virtually zero, further reducing wear on the valves and increasing their service life. 17 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au Pros and Cons of Alternatives

The harsh operating environments that exist throughout an acid plant result in the need for careful attention especially to reliability

engineering, materials selection, good operating principals and especially good maintenance regimes. 

Extensive downtime for sulphuric acid plants is really not an option for any company operating one.  In today’s booming nickel/cobalt market, this is especially true.  In most pyrometallurgical smelter complexes, loss of the acid plant would immediately necessitate shut down of the entire plant due to pollution concerns.  Where acid is used as a raw material (e.g. fertiliser industry, hydrometallurgical metals production such as nickel/cobalt) or regenerated in the chemical process industry, the interruption of raw materials would have an immediate effect on downstream processes.   Of particular note, in the metallurgical processing industry, there is a noticeable shift from acid producers (pyrometallurgical processes) to acid users (hydrometallurgical processes).   This is resulting in a reduction of available and relatively cheap smelter acid.  In turn there has been a large increase the value of sulphuric acid. 

Because of the issues noted, the drive to improve plant availability and avert catastrophes that could result in long term plant outage is of paramount importance to the industry.  Although some industries (such as the Florida fertiliser industry) have gone a long way to developing best practice, there is a need to consolidate these best practices across all industries, especially new hydrometallurgical plant operators now operating large sulphur burning plants. 

This paper looks at some best practice maintenance and operating procedures for sulphuric acid plants within the scope of mechanical integrity.  More specifically, it breaks down the analysis of the plant into six key elements: Environment, Operating Conditions, Age/History, Maintenance, Operators, Safety Devices, and Contingency Planning.  The overall goal is to define a good general best practice for the industry. 

###### 1. INTRODUCTION 

Sulphuric acid is an extremely important industrial chemical, probably one of the most important in the world.  Currently, about 37.9 million tonnes of sulphuric acid is produced worldwide.  So, this is an extremely critical chemical in manufacturing today.  It is used to manufacture a wide variety of other chemicals from fertilizers to pharmaceuticals.  It is also used in a variety of important production processes from impurity removal to metal ore leaching.  Approximately 70% of the sulphuric acid used is for the manufacture of fertilisers.  Most of this acid is produced by sulphur burning plants on-site.  The next most important producer would be the smelters, whose production ranges between 10-15% worldwide. 

Although demand for sulphuric acid had only been increasing at a rate of about 1% per year in the USA over the past several decades, it is now close to 10%. International figures are similar.  Subsequently, the price of acid has been driven up substantially (40% in 2004) and the high price and demand appears to be increasing

with further rises likely (but more likely on the 10% level).  This appears to be especially true with the apparent rise in demand in China.  The fertiliser industries in Florida, the traditional major consumers, have been expanding their own on-site capacity to make up for the decrease in both the supply of smelter and merchant acid and the subsequent price increases.  The usage of sulphuric acid in a range of new and different industries is also growing.  The growth of smaller speciality usage is about 3.5% per year.  Also, up until the late 1990’s, smelter acid production was increasing by about the same amount and actually reducing in many areas due to the low metal prices leading companies to shut a number of smelters.  This brings rise to another trend that is being noticed - the shift of smelter acid from primarily being sold to market, to being used for hydrometallurgical processes on site at the mines/smelters themselves.  This is not too surprising because the primary producer of smelter acid has

been the copper industry (about 90% of the total in the USA) and it is the heap leaching of copper ores is that is largely on the rise. 

The trend is being seen in the Nickel/Cobalt industry as well.  Heap leaching is being considered for Nickel production.  High pressure acid leaching processes, used primarily in the nickel/cobalt industry, are large users of acid.  The number of these plants is on the increase.  Going forward, it has been projected that the production of nickel from sulphide ores will remain more or less constant.  Most of the expansion in nickel production capacity over the next ten years will come from processing of laterite ores<sup>1</sup> , of which the bulk will use hydrometallurgical processes such as high pressure acid leaching HPAL for extraction. This seems quite logical when consideration is given to the fact that 70% of the world land based nickel resources are contained in laterite ores, but they only represent about 40% of the world production.  Also, there is no end in site to the growing usage of nickel, expected to maintain about a 4 percent per annum growth rate.  So, the daily acid usage is significant and the supply must be readily available, thus resulting in primarily on-site sulphur burning acid plants at these locations. 

As this paper is not focussed on the financial trends in the sulphuric acid industry, then what is the relevance of presenting this information?  The reason relates directly to risk management.  Although the safety and environmental aspects of the risks of these plants is critical, they do not stand alone from the business risks – primarily risk of business interruption as a result of an event that causes a plant shut down.  Such risks increase dramatically in surging markets like those now being seen with sulphuric acid. Risk can be defined as the product of frequency and consequence.  Both are affected dramatically in surging markets.

The increase in consequence is obvious – there are more dollars to be lost when the market price is high.  The increase in frequency may be less obvious, but it is there all the same.  With increasing prices, suppliers will push the plants harder; relax turnaround schedules, and do what is needed to increase production as much as possible.  New production plants that are built during these strong markets are built faster and brought on line quicker – both things that can increase the chance of an error in installation or early term operation.  These things are not limited to the sulphuric acid industry. They are trends that are noticed in all industries in strong market conditions.  With that said, their impact can be and often is drastically reduced or eliminated with good risk management.  And the cornerstone of good risk management for a chemical plant should be based on strong process safety management (PSM) principles. 

So, it is very important to acknowledge that a sulphuric acid plant is just that – a chemical plant.  The process of making sulphuric acid is based on three relatively straightforward equations: 



In the scope of chemistry, none of these reactions are overly complex.  However, controlling these relatively simple reactions is far from simple.  Sulphur dioxide and sulphuric acid are corrosive and difficult to handle, the sulphur trioxide intermediate is highly reactive and far from stable, and the amount of heat generated by these exothermic requires special consideration.
