###### 1 INTRODUCTION 

In 1998, Mintek presented a paper entitled “Resin-in-Pulp – After Au, Where Next?”<sup>i</sup> At that time, AIP (Adsorbent – in – Pulp) was widely used for the recovery of gold from slurries, because it eliminated the need for a solid – liqui

d separation step, which, because of the low ore grades, added significantly to the operating costs. Resin-in-Pulp (RIP) technology was developed shortly afterwards for use in the uranium and gold industries because of the superior performances of resins, compared to carbon. The main focus of the Mintek paper, however, was to investigate other applications for RIP, in particular the recovery of base metals from slurries. This seemed the logical continuation for RIP applications as various resins had already been identified for the removal of base metal impurities from solutions. However, base metal recovery from slurries presented its own challenges, which could not be resolved by simply applying knowledge gained from AIP in the gold and uranium industries. The main reason is the significantly higher base metals concentrations in slurries, i.e. upgrade ratios are significantly smaller resulting in shorter resin loading cycles and higher resin inventories. Base metal RIP systems therefore need to be able to: 1. Transfer resin more regularly 2. Transfer / handle resin more gently to minimise resin breakage (= losses) 3. Control resin concentrations in the various adsorption stages accurately to ensure low metal concentrations in the barren liquor. 4. Operate continuously to minimise the total resin inventory Carbon-in Pulp plants often use a carousel mode of operation to ensure improved carbon inventory management and minimised carbon handling. A carousel type operation of a RIP system is depicted in Figure 1. The design of such a system will often be restricted by physical constraints, e.g. in the case of low upgrades, large volumes of resin need to be drained out of the adsorption tanks into the elution columns. Bateman and Mintek joined forces in 2003 to address the above constraints. This effort culminated in the design of a continuous base metal RIP system, named MetRIX. FEED

This could be due to the low value of the metal-containing streams (e.g. slurry effluent streams) or due to the presence of ultra-fine or clay-like solids. Because it is important to assess upfront (i.e. at the conceptual design stage) whether the introduction of a MetRIX system will be economically viable, Bateman and Mintek have jointly developed economic models for two of the main MetRIX applications: MetRIX-E (MetRIX costing for Effluent Streams) evaluates the viability of a MetRIX system for the recovery of metals from effluent streams and slurries, and MetRIX-SL (MetRIX costing for Solid – Liquid Separation replacement) investigates the impact of the MetRIX system on overall process economics, where the MetRIX system partially replaces solid-liquid separation equipment. 4 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### 3.1 EFFLUENT TREATMENT (METRIX-E MODEL) One of the primary advantages of the MetRIX technology is its ability to reduce metal concentrations to low ppm levels. Base metal refineries often produce large volumes of effluents containing low concentrations of valuable metals. igh capital cost of the recovery process and/or high operating cost associated with these processes. Some of these ores have high clay content or have been ultra-fine milled. These pulps are difficult to settle or filter and solid-liquid separation is costly. Often metal losses to the filter cakes (or CCD underflows) are high as limited wash water can be accommodated in the water balance across the plant. Examples of these flow sheets include: - Ultra-fine grinding (to increase leach recoveries or to revert to less harsh leach conditions); - Bio-leach flow sheets; - Lateritic ores In general the solid-liquid separation steps in these flow sheets are CCD (counter-current decanter) circuits or belt-filter circuits or a combination of both. The separations have become more complex either due to the finer particles or due to the nature of the solids. Difficult solid – liquid separation are often characterised by lower thickening or filtration fluxes as well as increased moisture content in the CCD underflow or filtercake. Furthermore, the amount of wash water required to limit soluble losses and the type of solid-liquid separation will influence the size of the downstream processes (e.g. Fe removal, Co/Ni removal). A typical base metal refinery Flowsheet depicting the above is shown in Figure 10. A MetRIX system can be introduced into the flow sheet after the final solid-liquid separation step to reduce the soluble losses. Repulping of the filter cake or CCD underflow is done using part or all of the final plant raffinate. The eluate from the MetRIX system is returned to most suitable place in the primary plant. The flowsheet with the MetRIX technology is shown in Figure 11. Simply introducing a MetRIX system, without any modifications to the solid-liquid separation step will result in increased plant recoveries. ###### 1.0 INTRODUCTION 

PolyMet Mining Corp. (PolyMet) is advancing the development of the NorthMet Project.  The NorthMet deposit is located in northern Minnesota, adjacent to the historic Iron Range.  The deposit was discovered in the 1960’s and consists of a large, lower grade polymetallic sulfide deposit with values in Cu, Ni, Co, Zn, Au and Platinum Group Metals (PGM).  The NorthMet resource is estimated at > 900 million tons @ >0.90 Cu Equivalent grade at a 0.15% Cu cut off grade. 

PolyMet is currently completing a Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) with Bateman Engineering (Australia).  The study will include the mining, mineral processing and hydrometallurgical treatment of a bulk concentrate along with waste handling and disposal.  The processing site will be the former LTV Steel Mining Company taconite iron ore processing plant which is located about 7 miles from the NorthMet deposit.  The plant and associated mining operations were closed in early 2001 due to bankruptcy and at its peak, this plant processed over 90,000 long tons/day of taconite iron ore via a four stage crushing, grinding and flotation process.  PolyMet is now the owner of this plant (purchase was completed in 2005) and plans to reactivate sufficient capacity to treat 32,000 short tons per day of NorthMet ore to produce a bulk sulfide flotation concentrate for further treatment using the PLATSOL™ process. 

The DFS program has included pilot scale testwork at SGS Lakefield Research Limited in Ontario, Canada.  Pilot plant tests have been performed on ore flotation to produce bulk concentrate samples and on hydrometallurgical treatment of the bulk concentrate materials.  Two variants of the hydrometallurgical process were tested.  The “base case” flowsheet involves high temperature chloride-assisted leaching (PLATSOL™), solid-liquid separation and washing, PGM/Au precipitation, neutralization, Cu SX/EW to produce copper cathode.  The two variants, driven by offtake interest, include two different routes to nickel, cobalt, and zinc recovery.  The first variation treats a portion of the Cu SX raffinate (remainder is recycled to the autoclave) sequentially by neutralization, first and second stage iron/aluminum removal, residual copper removal by precipitation as a sulfide,  first stage Ni/Co/Zn precipitation with magnesia, second stage Ni/Co/Zn precipitation with lime and then magnesium removal with lime.  The product from this first variation is a “mixed” hydroxide of nickel, cobalt and zinc. 

The second variation again treats a portion of the Cu SX raffinate sequentially

by neutralization, first and second stage iron/aluminum removal and residual copper sulfide precipitation.  The Cu-Fe-Al free solution is then processed by Co/Zn solvent extraction (with Cyanex 272) with selective zinc and cobalt stripping, cobalt precipitation with magnesia, nickel (purified raffinate stream after Co/Zn SX) precipitation with magnesia, secondary precipitation of residual nickel with lime and finally magnesium precipitation with lime.  The products from this second variation are a zinc sulfate strip solution (to a zinc off-take), a cobalt hydroxide precipitate and a nickel hydroxide precipitate. 

The final choice between the mixed and purified hydroxide route for nickel and cobalt products will be based on final cost analysis and market surveys. 

The following paper provides an overview of the current project and results from the pilot testing. 

###### 2.0 NORTHMET PROJECT 

The NorthMet Project is located in northeastern Minnesota, near the Mesabi Iron Range and 6 miles south of the town of Babbitt. Figure 1 shows the location on a map of North America. 

PolyMet has a 100% leasehold interest for the mineral rights on the 4,162 acres that make up the NorthMet property. The infrastructure is excellent. Available to the Project are low-cost power, well developed roads and railway networks, and supply-equipment centers that support the numerous operating iron ore mines, the nearest being two miles from NorthMet. There is an abundant supply of skilled labor locally. 

The NorthMet deposit is believed to be the largest undeveloped non-ferrous metal project in the U.S. It is a polymetallic magmatic sulfide deposit containing platinum, palladium, gold, copper, nickel, cobalt, and silver, hosted near the base of the Duluth Mafic Complex.

The crushing and grinding circuits are existing circuits within the “Cliff’s Erie” plant and will only utilize a small portion of the available capacity. 

The flotation circuit is designed to produce a bulk concentrate carrying pay metals and a tailing with low residual sulfur content.  The float circuit has the following elements;

The temperature range for total pressure oxidation is typically 220 to 230°C.  The autoclave discharge from the leach process contains dissolved Cu, Ni, Co, Zn, Au, Pt and Pd.  The solids are relatively “barren” of value, consisting of iron precipitates, unreacted gangue and minor amounts of residual base and precious metal minerals. 

The original PLATSOL® pilot plant utilized a “straight through” design [1] in which fresh concentrate was introduced into the first compartment of a 6-compartment pilot autoclave with raffinate (for controlled cooling of the autoclave slurry) and oxygen (for oxidation).  The results of the “straight through” pilot plant indicated that virtually all the copper and nickel were extracted in the first compartment of the autoclave due to the rapidity of the sulfide oxidation process.  However, the platinum and palladium minerals continued to react through the entire autoclave volume, reaching ultimate extractions of about 95%.  This situation was revisited in the more recent bench and pilot scale testing.  It was concluded that a “recycle’ design would be more efficient with respect to autoclave design.  The “recycle” design involves thickening the autoclave discharge and recycling a portion of the underflow to the autoclave feed.  This recycle allows for any unreacted mineral to have a chance at second-pass extraction.  The greater the recycle, the longer the “average” residence time of solids in the autoclave.  The limit of the recycle will be when the solids density in the autoclave becomes unmanageable.

###### 4.6 Raffinate Neutralization 

The purpose of raffinate neutralization is to trim the acid level in the copper raffinate prior to splitting the raffinate flow between the nickel and cobalt recovery circuit and returning the raffinate to the autoclave circuit as a cooling solution.  Acid must be neutralized prior to the nickel and cobalt recovery process steps and excess acid is undesirable in the feed to the autoclave as excess acid will increase the formation of basic ferric sulfate in the autoclave solids. 

The chemistry of raffinate neutralization is the same as the primary neutralization discussed above. 

###### 4.7 Fe and Al Removal 

The removal of iron and aluminum prior to recovery of nickel and cobalt is necessary to prevent product contamination. 

The process of iron oxy-hydrolysis is well known.  Iron is oxidized from the ferrous to the ferric state with oxygen or air with limestone addition for neutralization and pH control.  The temperature for iron removal was set to 60 °C and the pH to 3.0.  The iron was removed to less than 5 mg/L by this process with negligible losses of Ni/Co to the iron precipitate residue. 

Similar results were obtained in the pilot plant using limestone to pH 4.6-4.7 and 65 °C.  Terminal aluminum levels were 38 mg/L on average. 

The iron precipitate is washed and disposed to tailings.  The aluminum precipitate is thickened and recycled to the iron removal step. 

###### 4.8 Copper Removal 

Residual copper is removed before nickel, cobalt and zinc recovery using NaSH precipitation.  The copper sulfide product (synthetic covellite) is then recycled internally to precipitate gold and PGM from the autoclave discharge solution. 

The chemistry is straightforward; 

###### CuSO4 + NaSH = CuS + 0.5Na2SO4 + 0.5H2SO4 

In the 2005 pilot plant, the copper level in solution advancing to copper removal was reduced to less than 50 mg/L.

The NorthMet ore and concentrate contains some magnesium silicate mineralization.  During high temperature autoclave leaching of the concentrate, some magnesium is leached. The resultant loss of practical knowledge and experience impacts detrimentally on ultimate plant ramp-up time and operating efficiencies. One approach to assist resource companies in dealing with this issue is the use of custom-built interactive models of various types that together provide both a training and simulation framework to aid the decision-making process. Integration of process parameter calculations with computational fluid dynamic and 3D animations can provide a powerful and effective base for the ongoing capture of metallurgical plant performance prediction and rapid knowledge transfer to newly assigned staff. One component is examined in this design-stage case study. It aims at providing an estimate of technical and economic efficiencies that may result from replacing a given number of counter-current decantation (CCD) stages in a virtual nickel laterite or sulfide plant with a resin-in-pulp (RIP) metals-scavenging circuit. Potential benefits may include reduced capital expenditure and improved metal recoveries. Experience that has been gained in the engineering and operation of resin-in-pulp plants for gold would provide a sound basis for this application, along with the appropriate selection of resin type. Determination of the optimal number of stages to curtail the CCD circuit depends on several factors, not least of which is the resin capaci

ty, which in turn impacts on resin inventory and turnover for a given slurry composition and flow. 

The economics of using of RIP as a scavenger on the back end of a 2, 3 or 4-stage CCD compare favourably with a conventional 6-stage CCD circuit, depending on operational issues such as the possible recovery of some of the Ni and Co that is lost in a conventional circuit by co-precipitation, and the scavenging of spikes in tailings Ni/Co tenors resulting from circuit upsets.  There is no benefit to retrofitting an existing CCD circuit with a RIP plant if plant upset conditions are ignored; however, even a comparatively small net effect of plant upset would be beneficial under the conditions used in the case study; four CCD stages would suffice, followed by a 2-stage RIP plant of suitable size to handle the pulp flowrate. 

This simulation and modelling study has demonstrated that the notion of a hybrid CCD-RIP circuit has potential benefit, particularly for new plants at design stage.  More detailed selection of circuit configuration can be made at the feasibility study level by use of simulations with consideration of testwork data.  For retrofit of existing plants, CCD circuit performance is a major factor in the decision-making process. 

###### 1. INTRODUCTION 

The current economic boom in the minerals sector coupled with decreased student numbers in the minerals processing and metallurgical areas over the last few years, has introduced strain on both design and operations management of extractive metallurgical plants.  Demand for skilled metallurgical staff has engendered ease of movement between operations, as individuals take up opportunities to broaden their experience base via short-term contracts, as well as what can be significant financial incentives for shortterm overseas contracts on remote minesites.  Provision of interactive training information packs to operating staff is one way to address the issue of continual operating strategy handovers. 

A further impact of the currently elevated metals prices is a tendency for some resource companies engaged in engineering development of process plants to favour older but less cost-efficient technologies simply because the current financial model allows it.  This short-term view tends to overlook the possibility of metals prices undergoing a correction or downturn in the longer term, at which time being locked in to inflexible and less efficient technologies may have dire consequences.  Process modeling techniques are generally utilized at the design stage as a shortcut to calculating material balance data for the definitive process flowsheet, rather than as a full-blown predictive tool aiding the selection of techno-economic process options. 

Once the plant has reached the commissioning stage, slow ramp-up to design setpoints and targets has often been flagged as a problem area, particularly for more complex hydrometallurgical circuits (Reid and Barnett, 2002; Nice, 2002; Campbell, 2004

). Modules integrating interactive training information with process modelling would provide a guide to assist process engineers and metallurgists to more readily meet target ramp-up periods. 

This paper is the first in a series directed at the concept of a virtual metallurgical plant as one tool that may be useful in addressing these issues.  The information technology revolution has provided a range of computer-based modelling and simulation methodologies to metallurgists and engineers, from the use of simple spreadsheets for deriving plant operating data through to complex computational fluid dynamic simulations for the visualization and derivation of velocity and temperature vector plane data.

The case study in this work considers the ramifications of systematically replacing CCD stages in a virtual nickel laterite or sulfide plant with a RIP metals-scavenging circuit, to assess the potential techno-economic benefits. 

###### 2. CCD vs RIP 

Hydrometallurgical processing of both sulfidic and lateritic nickel ores typically incorporates solid-liquid separation using CCD, usually comprising up to seven large-scale thickeners in series with a counter-current process water wash.  Given the high cost of autoclave leaching, CCD circuits are designed to ensure the efficient recovery of metal values from the autoclave residue slurry under both typical and upset conditions. Given the acidity of the slurry, extensive corrosion-resistant material is required for the CCD circuit and can therefore represent a significant capital cost, as well as operating cost. Moreover, nickel laterite slurries often contain clay phases and the resultant viscosity can present problems with efficient settling or filtration of the solids, resulting in the loss of metal values to tailings underflow. 

Consideration of the stagewise metal-recovery duty for a typical CCD circuit reveals that the majority (>90%) of the nickel and cobalt is typically recovered in the first two or three stages, with the following four or five stages acting as scavengers for the remaining ~10% of the va

lue metals, as shown later in this paper.  This fact elicits the question of whether the back end of the CCD circuit could feasibly be replaced with a less costly unit process that is specifically designed for scavenging, rather than thickening. 

According to Reid and Barnett (2002), the Murrin Murrin, Bulong and Cawse nickel laterite projects all experienced greater than anticipated losses in the CCD and subsequent stages in the first years of operation, making overall recoveries to saleable product significantly lower than design levels. 

Resin-based technologies, in the form of continuous counter-current ion-exchange (CCIX) and resin-in-pulp, have been used in metallurgical process plants for many years. Polymer beads containing functional groups to which Ni and Co moieties are attracted, are contacted with the solution (CCIX) or slurry (RIP) to scavenge these metals, which are later stripped from the resin for recovery.  In the case of RIP there is no need for solid-liquid separation, and the resin is recovered by screening.  This makes RIP a potentially attractive candidate to replace the back end of the CCD circuit. 

While resins have long been used in the uranium industry in a CCIX context, their use in a RIP configuration has thus far been directed mainly at the recovery of gold (Kotze, et al., 2005).  The former Soviet Union and its subsequent countries recovered a substantial proportion of their collectively large gold production by RIP over the past thirty years. With the advent of several commercial gold-selective resins, there are RIP plants now operating at Penjom, Malaysia and Barbrook, South Africa.  Moreover, a gold-selective resin is now also being offered commercially as part of a unit operation for the recovery of gold from the intensive cyanide leaching of gravity products. 

Resins already feature significantly in downstream purification and refining circuits associated with nickel/cobalt processing plants.  CCIX as well as single or dual-stage columns are commonly found in these circuits for various duties.  Resins are used for the removal of Zn from Ni or Co streams, Ni from Co streams and Co from Ni streams, for example. 

Potential application of RIP to the recovery of nickel and cobalt has been mentioned in overview by Taylor and Jansen (2000), who cite the fact that CCD circuits involve significant capital and operating costs, occupy large footprint areas, and require a significant quantity of wash water, which dilutes the feed to the associated Ni/Co recovery facilities.  These authors propose a flowsheet whereby the RIP stage becomes the primary recovery unit process, replacing the CCD circuit completely as well as conventional downstream mixed sulfide precipitation (MSP), mixed hydroxide precipitation (MHP) or solvent extraction (SX) circuits. Final recovery would be by electrowinning (EW) or hydrogen reduction.  This circuit configuration is considered as one of several in the current study. 

Zontov (2001) disc

usses the application of a proprietary resin (R604) to RIP for Ni/Co.  In the case of autoclave residue slurries, the pH is adjusted to ~4, to remove both ferric and ferrous iron.  In this process, significant Ni (~15%) as well as Co is lost by precipitation; however, more than half of the precipitated Ni and Co is recovered onto the resin during the RIP process.  The second case of scavenging from conventional CCD tailings was also examined and found to yield similar results.  The author also speculates that a hybrid CCD-RIP circuit could be useful, although no data is given.

Wyethe, et al. (2002) considered the recovery of Co, Ni and Cu from CCD underflow, via a dual RIP system operating at pH ~3 for Cu, followed by a second RIP train operating at pH ~4.5, for Ni and Co recovery.  This was adopted to minimize Cu losses by precipitation at pH 4.5, the optimal pH value for Ni and Co recovery. The single-train option for simultaneous recovery of all three elements, operating at a pH value of ~4, resulted in greater than 99% Ni and Co recoveries, along with 77% Cu recovery. 

Tatarnikov, et al. (2002) opted for the replacement of conventional recovery processes for Ni, Co and Cu, with ion-exchange of solid/liquid separated liquors.  Cu was recovered with TPE249 resin, while Ni and Co were recovered using TPE247. 

###### 2.1. RESIN SELECTION 

A resin is required that is capable of extracting the nickel and cobalt with a reasonable degree of selectivity, so that the resin loading is not suppressed by another element.  Pre-neutralization will be effective in removing ferric iron; however, the resin should be reasonable selective against other moieties such as Fe<sup>2+</sup> , Al<sup>3+</sup> , etc. 

Metzner and Arnall (2002) describe the efforts of one manufacturer in their quest for elevated selectivity for resins in base-metal systems.  The applications cited are from clear solutions by carousel CCIX, rather than from slurries by RIP, however. 

While commercial Ni-selective resins do not currently exist, there are several chelating resins currently widely used in water treatment that have been used for co-recovery of Ni and Co to obtain an intermediate product.  Monospherical, abrasion-resistant resins have also been made commercially available by some manufacturers, and these would be well suited to RIP duty.  The iminodiacetic functional group has been used by several manufacturers to provide resins (eg, Lewatit TP207; Purolite S-930) that are reasonably selective for Ni and Co and where metal values can be recovered by acid elution. 

###### 2.2. RIP EQUIPMENT SELECTION 

Commercially operating RIP plants generally comprise (i) sieve bend / airlift systems installed in a series of tanks with interstage screens, where resin is transferred stagewise, counter-currently to the flow of pulp (Wyethe, et al., 2002), and (ii) the AAC Pumpcell plants, which operate in a carousel system, requiring no direct

transfer of resin from one tank to the next during the adsorption stage (Anon., 2003; Rogans et al,1996, 2002). There are several implications of the different operating methodogies resulting from equipment selection. Resin transfer and handling time is minimized in the case of the AAC Pumpcell, but more must be allowed for in the sieve bend / airlift option. Compressed air is required for the latter. The former can operate at higher resin concentrations, shrinking the size of the plant. Equipment selection is best made on the basis of a sound techno-economic evaluation of the particular application. ###### 2.3. In the experience of this author, adsorbents such as resins and carbons may undergo contact adsorption with solid-bound metal species, enabling the recovery of values that are otherwise lost. Fin

ally, an advantage to having a RIP scavenger circuit is its ability to ‘mop up’ spikes in tailings Ni/Co tenors resulting from circuit upsets owing to thickener rat-holing or bogging, over or underdosing of flocculant, washwater or underflow pumping issues, etc. Moreover, sporadic feeding of anomalously high-clay ores can result in poor CCD wash efficiencies and long periods of high soluble losses. 

###### 3. SIMULATION RESULTS 

The aim of this work is not to exhaustively review the engineering design and chemistry of the proposed CCD-RIP hybrid circuit, but rather to provide an overview based on simple modelling and assumptions, for conceptualization and visualization purposes.  By their nature, mineral processing operations are orebody and site-specific and hence, the potential for application of any other process flowsheet modification should be evaluated using application-specific design and metallurgical data. 

###### 3.1. BASE CASE 

Base case conditions were selected based on the relatively high throughput parameters cited in Zontov (2001), representative of the plant size that may be required to benefit from economies of scale.  The conditions cited by Mayze (1999) were also considered. The base case conditions are summarized in Table 1.  A 10% rate of Ni co-precipitation is assumed for the pre-neutralization step, and 50% of this Ni is assumed to be recoverable in the RIP process.  To simplify the calculation, for our purposes it is assumed that 5% of the dissolved Ni is lost to tailings irreversibly as co-precipitate during pre-neutralization. 

To further simplify the calculation, only Ni is considered and Co, Cu and other elements are ignored.

CONCLUSIONS The potential benefit of ‘virtual plant’ techno-economic process simulation is demonstrated at the design level, but is also applicable to operational-level applications. While complete replacement of the entire CCD circuit with an RIP plant may entail lower capital costs, operating cost considerations with 5-year capital amortization suggest that the use of RIP as a scavenger on the back end of a 3-stage CCD compares favourably with those of a conventional 6-stage CCD circuit. ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au 11 The outcome is further influenced on consideration of operational issues such as the possible recovery of some of the Ni and Co that is lost in a conventional circuit owing to adsorption onto solids or co-precipitation with iron or aluminium, and the scavenging of spikes in tailings Ni/Co tenors resulting from circuit upsets (thickener rat-holing or bogging, flocculant dosing control, pumping and rheology issues). By decreasing the CCD circuit to between 2 and 4 stages and adding a scavenging RIP circuit of the appropriate size, resultant Ni credits would yield a significant cost benefit to the operation, particularly if the slurry is expected to have rheological or settling difficulties. Appropriate bench and pilot-scale testing of these expected real-world operational and orebody issues is therefore critical to enable these factors to be duly inclu

ded in the techno-economic analysis. 

Future developments in the processing of nickel such as atmospheric leaching, as well as the integration of pressure acid and atmospheric leaching, such as the EPAL® process currently being constructed for the Ravensthorpe operation (Adams, et al., 2004), will render both the mineral and solution chemistry different again.  Upstream changes on CCD and RIP chemistry and mineral phases affect flocculation, settling characteristics, solution species, co-precipitation and other factors. 

There is a potential further environmental benefit to application of a hybrid CCD-RIP circuit to Ni/Co processing, owing to the reduction in entrained and adsorbed heavy metals deporting to tailings, with concomitant reduction in heavy metal runoff. 

There is no benefit to retrofitting an existing CCD circuit with a RIP plant if plant upset conditions are ignored; however, even a comparatively small net effect of plant upset would be beneficial under the conditions used in the case study; four CCD stages would suffice, followed by a 2-stage RIP plant of suitable size to handle the pulp flowrate. 

This simulation and modelling study has demonstrated that the notion of a hybrid CCD-RIP circuit has potential benefit, particularly for new plants at design stage. More detailed selection of circuit configuration can be made at the feasibility study level by use of simulations with consideration of testwork data.  For retrofit of existing plants, CCD circuit performance is a major factor in the decision-making process.

###### 1. ABSTRACT 

A dynamic model has been developed for analysing and predicting the performance of metallurgical process plants.  The model takes into account the factors that influence production on a dynamic basis, including ore grades, throughput capacity, equipment reliability and surge capacity. 

The model has been applied to several hydrometallurgical flowsheets for design verification, surge optimisation and identification of production bottlenecks.  This paper tracks the development of the model, describes its operation and proposes future applications. 

###### 2. INTRODUCTION 

Complex metallurgical processes can be analysed quickly and effectively using simulation models. Recent innovations provide a powerful tool for evaluating flowsheets, taking into account the key economic drivers over the whole operating life of a project.  Mine plans, metallurgical characteristic models, equipment reliability statistics and surge capacities are all considered in an integrated plant dynamic model.  The result is lower risk and greater confidence in engineering decision making. 

Plant designs are commonly based on a steady state mass and energy balance model of the flowsheet.  These give a simplistic ‘perfect world’ snapshot.  Real world fluctuations are conveniently ignored, creating the illusion of a stable, steady process.  Dynamic models bring the mass and energy balance to life with real plant limitations and instabilities. 

Simulus first developed a dynamic transfer model to meet a client’s specific needs.  The client, operating a complex nickel hydrometallurgical process, was embarking on expansion and optimisation studies and needed a tool to evaluate the various alternatives.  The plant was characterised by: 

- Poor equipment reliability in some areas 

- Mismatched area throughput capacities 

- Limited inter-stage surge capacity 

- Parallel production trains (existing and proposed) 

- Complex interactions between plant stages (multiple recycles) • Utility and reagent supply constraints 

The dynamic interactions of throughput capacity, equipment reliability, and surge capacity caused the production bottleneck to shift from point to point.  The impact of capital projects could not be accurately predicted by steady state modelling.  In some cases throughput improvements were rendered inconsequential by the quite daunting reliability issues.  These problems were overcome by developing a whole-plant simulation tool. 

The Simulus Dynamic Model overlays the mass and energy balance with real equipment characteristics and dynamic fluctuations.  The simulated plant can be run for a period of several years, with all major economic drivers considered on a dynamic basis: 

- Ore grades 

- Area by area throughput capacity 

- Equipment failure statistics 

- Planned maintenance schedules 

- Surge capacity 

- Utility and reagent supply 

The resulting models give a far more realistic simulation of plant operation and are becoming a fund

amental tool in design and optimisation of process facilities. ###### 3. DEALING WITH COMPLEXITY Consider the simple process shown in Figure 1. This operation has the potential to be the first commercial scale nickel bacterial heap leaching operation in the world. In addition the bacterial culture that will be inoculated into the heaps will be saline tolerant as the water supply at Sherlock Bay is saline with a salt concentration similar to that of seawater. Results presented from laboratory testwork demonstrate rapid leaching kinetics of the ore in saline waters thus negating the need for incorporating a desalination plant into the commercial operation design. This paper will discuss the results that have been obtained from testing the numerous ore samples and will describe the application of the BioHeap™ process to heap leaching of the ore from the Sherlock Bay Nickel Deposit. ###### 1.0 INTRODUCTION Conventional treatment of sulphide ores has predominantly focused on floating the ore to produce a concentrate which is then smelted or roasted followed by acid leaching and refining to produce metal. Importantly sulphide ores normally contain trace levels of mercury, tellurium, selenium and arsenic. These impurities were traditionally emitted into the atmosphere or alternatively entered the process gases used to make sulphuric acid. Processes have been developed to cope with these hazards, eg electrostatic precipitators and wet scrubbers, however these add significantly to the operating costs of the smelters. Due to ever increasing environmental awareness smelters are now, either voluntarily or through legislation, reducing the levels of sulphur dioxide gas emitted into the environment resulting in the eyes of the mineral processing industry looking to other more socially/environmentally acceptable means of processing the ores (Williams et al 1999). Over recent years much research has been aimed at developing hydrometallurgical alternatives to the established pyrometallurgical processes. These include various autoclave based technologies such as Western Metal’s Mt Gordon process (Weir, 1999), the Activox Process and the CESL process. Other hydrometallurgical sulphide processing routes have been developed involving the use of a halide leaching lixiviant; one such example is the Intec Copper process which utilises a bromochl

oride brine to leach copper from ores and their concentrates.  Although the Sherritt process is not a new technology it is a hydrometallurgical ammonia based leach. 

Bacterial leaching has been employed, either intentionally or otherwise, for the leaching of sulphide ores since as early as 1000BC when copper was recovered from liquor streams which had passed through mining operations and ore bodies (Brierley et al 1985).  Bacterial leaching offers an economical method of processing sulphide ores and their concentrates including refractory gold, copper, nickel, zinc, cobalt and other sulphide ores (Harvey, 2003).  There are five general types of bacterial leaching options for processing sulphide ores and concentrates; these are tank leaching, vat leaching, dump leaching, in situ leaching and heap leaching. 

Tank leaching takes place in temperature controlled stirred aerated tanks which contain the bacterial culture and ground mineral slurry.  The tanks may be mechanically stirred or the method of aeration may also be used to perform the agitation as is the case in a pachuca. 

Vat leaching is often employed as an alternative to heap leaching in areas of high rainfall where excessive dilution of leachate can occur because of the large area exposed on the heap.  The process consists of constructing a vat structure into which crushed or ground and agglomerated ore is placed.  The vats may be constructed in areas that may have been previously approved for tailings dams, within exhausted pits, or at other suitable sites.  Like heaps the vats are lined and can be covered to prevent ingress of water from rainfall events.  There is often a crude aeration system incorporated into the vat.  Solution is pumped into the vat through a series of pipes or channels in the base until the ore is completely saturated.  After passing through the ore the leachate is drawn off and passed into downstream processing.

Dump leaching is a form of heap leaching where run-of-mine ore is stacked directly onto a prepared pad without prior crushing and may be extended to include large valley fill facilities (Smith, M. E., 2002). 

In situ leaching or solution mining is a process whereby metals are removed from an ore deposit; it differs from heap leaching as the ore is kept in the ground or in situ.  Holes are drilled into the ore body and a lixiviant is pumped into the holes.  As the lixiviant passes through the ore body the metals are dissolved and the pregnant liquor is then pumped up from the base of the leaching zone to a surface plant. 

Heap leaching involves stacking run-of-mine or crushed whole ore onto engineered pads.  Heaps are irrigated with acidic solutions and the leached metal reports to these solutions as it drains from the base of the heap.  The bacteria employed in heap leaching are generally aerobic and therefore require oxygen which may be forced into the heap by means of low pressure blowers or air may be suck

ed into the heap due to a chimney effect that occurs as bacteria oxidise ore and create heat. The BioHeap™ process is a variation of a standard heap leach. 

BioHeap Limited has developed a direct bio-leach process in which chemical attack by ferric does not play a significant role.  As a result, the leach does not require extreme temperatures, nor does it require fine grinding.  As such the process is just as applicable to heap leaching as it is to tanks or any of the above alternatives.  However, BioHeap Ltd has focussed its technology more so to the treatment of whole ore in heaps.  To date the group has developed methods for the treatment of refractory gold ores, copper bearing chalcopyrite and chalcopyrite/gold ores, zinc ores, lead/zinc ores and nickel ores. 

One of the main areas of focus for the BioHeap group has been the development of a saline tolerant bacterial culture capable of operating in waters found within Western Australia with a particular emphasis on the water found in the Eastern Goldfields.  Here water can sometimes be up to eight times the salinity of seawater.  It is one of these saline tolerant bacterial cultures that has been applied to the leaching of the Sherlock Bay ore as the water supply at this site is of a similar salinity to that of seawater. 

This paper describes the application of the BioHeap™ process to the heap leaching of the Sherlock Bay Nickel ore deposit in the Pilbara region of Western Australia.

###### 2.1 STAGE 1 

Amenability Testing determines the compatibility of the BioHeap bacteria to the specific mineralogy of the ore from the Sherlock Bay mine, and determines what, if any, potential toxins are present in the ore.  Amenability testing also incorporates some metallurgical diagnostic testwork such as mineralogy and Nitric Acid Digestion (NADs) which examines the sulphide liberation of the mineral at a series of different crush sizes. 

###### 2.2 STAGE 2 

Column leach testing involves determining the optimum agglomeration conditions for the crushed ore then leaching these in a column over a period of months. 

During a heap leach it is imperative that the integrity of the heap is maintained and that pore spaces between the ore particles are kept open so that aeration and irrigation of the heap take place to an optimum level.  If the agglomerates within the heap fail then the heap slumps causing pore spaces to block and thus preventing the flow of air and solution to this area of the heap the result is a loss of leaching efficiency in the failed area of the heap. 

Before column leach testing can take place it is vital to first determine the best conditions for agglomerating the ore which involves binding the fine particles with the larger ones generated during crushing the ore.  A series of agglomeration trials are run using water and acid in different proportions as the binding agents, very occasionally the addition of binders is needed to form stable agglomerates.  Once agglomerates are formed they are cured and loaded into a column where they are subjected to stringent slump and percolation tests in order to determine the strength of the agglomerates. 

Once agglomeration is optimized, a batch of ore is agglomerated, inoculated with the especially adapted proprietary bacterial culture, selected during Stage 1, before being loaded into the column where leaching begins.  Monitoring of the column takes place regularly over a period of months with samples and measurements of pH, ORP and metal contents reporting to solution being recorded. The progression of the leach is plotted on a recovery curve with the data being the levels of metal reporting to solution.  The curve generated from the data points generally allows BioHeap Ltd to make an estimate of the leaching cycle time that would be expected at a full scale operation. 

###### 2.3 STAGE 3 

The tertiary stage of testing involves operating larger scale columns in the laboratory.  Usually a number of columns are utilized in order to optimize a number of leach parameters, such as crush size, method of inoculation, operating pH’s, and whether forced aeration is required in full scale heaps.  Variability testing of ore samples from various locations within the ore deposit is also usually completed at this time, depending upon the availability of the ore, but as a minimum, an ore blend incorporating a representative suite of drill co

re samples is used for the optimisation testwork. 

Monitoring of these columns takes place in much the same way as those in Stage 2.

The final testwork stage is large scale, on site, piloting, with a heap of between 5000 and 100,000 tonnes.  A heap of this size simulates, very closely, the characteristics of a full scale commercial operation, but in a more controlled manner.

###### 3.2 GEOLOGY 

The Sherlock Bay nickel sulphide deposit is unusual in that it is not contained within ultramafic rocks that are generally associated with nickel sulphides.  The enclosing rocks for the Sherlock Bay deposit are predominantly intermediate and acid volcanic rocks with minor gabbro and basalt.  The strike of the mineralised horizon and the enclosing rocks is ENE; the dips are steep north, overturning to steep south at depth.  An ultramafic hill outcrops adjacent to the mineralised horizon and is the probable source of the nickel sulphides.  The mineralised horizon outcrops at the western shoot (Discovery) as a highly siliceous banded iron formation.  The eastern shoot (Symond’s Well) is covered by transported soils, clays and gravels up to 10m thick.  At depth the mineralised horizon is a black siliceous chert with amounts of amphibole.  True widths of mineralisation range up to 40m.

One of the proprietary saline tolerant bacterial cultures that had been grown on nickel ores was selected for use in the test. The bacteria responsible for leaching sulphide ores are usually composed of iron oxidising bacteria, such at Thiobacillus ferrooxidans and Leptospirillum ferrooxidans, and sulphur oxidisers such as Thiobacillus ferrooxidans and Sulfolobus thermosulfidooxidans for example. The bacteria 8 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au predominant within the BioHeap™ bacterial cultures are sulphur oxidisers. These bacteria metabolise reduced sulphur species with the most reduced sulphur species being oxidised in preference and in order to the more oxidised sulphur species. Thus sulphides are oxidised to form elemental sulphur and then elemental sulphur is oxidised to form sulphate. Like most organisms the bacteria will do the least amount of work to achieve the maximum results.

Thus for mixed metal sulphides, the sulphides that are more readily oxidised and less refractory in structure, such as pentlandite and chalcocite, will be oxidised in preference to those sulphides that are more refractory such as chalcopyrite. The leaching curves plotting the metal values reporting to solution show this pattern quite obviously. Nickel, contained in pentlandite, leaches first and only when the leaching rate of nickel slows does the rate of chalcopyrite oxidation, illustrated by the copper values reporting to solution, increase. The curves show which minerals are preferentially attacked by the bacterial cultures. As leaching progresses the sulphides exposed during crushing become less prevalent at the surface of the mineral and often the bacteria are required to ‘burrow’ further into the ore to reach more sulphides essential for their metabolism. At the point where the leaching rate slows the columns are taken down and blended, sub-sampled and assayed then re-loaded into the columns and leaching is re-commenced. The columns are re-established with the same irrigation rates and aeration rates and leaching continues. Often the levels of metal reporting to solution increase as precipitates are exposed and any channels formed during the first phase of leaching are removed during the re-stacking process, thus allowing a uniform progression of lixiviant to pass through the column ensuring all solids are wet. Once leaching slows again the column is drained then rinsed with acidified water and water before being dismantled and the residues weighed and assayed in order to perform the final mass balance. ###### 5.1 ACID GENERATION USING LEACH RESIDUE 

The following is a brief discussion on the logic behind each of the proposed column tests. 

###### 5.1.1 Sulphur addition 

The bacterial culture added to the column leaches was grown specifically to oxidise reduced forms of sulphur.  Once the most reduced form of sulphur, in the case of the Sherlock Bay ore this is sulphide, is depleted the bacterial culture then attacks the next most reduced sulphur species which would be elemental sulphur.  When sulphur is oxidised it forms sulphates one of which is hydrogen sulphate or sulphuric acid.  The theory behind establishing one of the columns was that the sulphide leaching had nearly ceased so the bacterial culture should be switching from oxidising sulphides as their feed source to oxidising elemental sulphur.  If, at this point in their life cycle, elemental sulphur were to be blended with the bacterially populated spent sulphide leach residue, perhaps the bacteria would metabolise the added sulphur to generate sulphuric acid according to reaction 1. 

One way of reducing acid consumption within the heap is through the oxidation of elemental sulphur to sulphuric acid via the following reaction: S<sup>0</sup> +  H2O  +  1½ O2  →  H2SO4 (1) 

Elemental sulphur could be added to the ore to promote sulphuric acid generation; this theory was tested in column 1. 

###### 5.1.2. Extended Irrigation Cycle 

This test was a continuation of the original to see if the heap would eventually become acid generating.  Any remaining elemental sulphur generated from oxidation of the sulphide and any pyrite remaining in the residue may further oxidise to produce acid. 

Once the column containing the Symond’s Well residue crushed to 6.3 mm had completed leaching the residue was blended and split to form two portions, one portion was blended with elemental sulphur at a level of 33kg/t of residue.  This blend was loaded into a column and irrigated with standard nutrient solution made up in saline water. 

The second column contained the spent residue but was irrigated with the pregnant liquor generated from leaching the sulphide ore; this was in a saline environment.  In commercial practice irrigation of old heaps continues as these tend to become acid producing as the remaining sulphides and elemental sulphur is oxidised. 

The Symond’s Well 6.3

mm column was assayed for sulphur species at the conclusion of nickel and copper leaching. Using the assays of elemental sulphur and sulphide sulphur present in the residue, the amount of sulphuric acid that could be generated by extended irrigation was calculated. Analysis of the residue reported levels of elemental sulphur present within the residue at 1.80%. A mass of 7335.5g was added to the column which means that according to reaction (1) and assuming that all the sulphur was available for reaction, approximately 404g of sulphuric acid could be generated by the oxidation of the remaining elemental sulphur alone in the heap. Analysis of the sulphide sulphur present in the leached residue indicated that 0.66% was present. Sulphide is oxidised according to the following reaction (2) followed by reaction (1). According to these reactions approximately 148g of sulphuric acid should be generated from the sulphide sulphur and 404g from the elemental sulphur present in the residue assuming all sulphur and sulphide is liberated for reaction. ###### ABSTRACT 

Heap leaching to treat nickel sulfide and laterite has been studied. The tests were done in laboratory and pilot plant.  The process has been used in commercial scale in China.  This paper summarized the results of tests and described the flowsheet.  The operating cost has been indicated.

- Reduce transportation facilities such roads and port size 

- Reduce manpower and facilities related.

TREATMENT OF NICKEL SULPHIDE ORE The traditional process for the treatment of nickel sulphide ore is mineral processing - smelting - converting - refining. The emerging processes on the hydrometallurgical side are mainly pressure leaching and bioheap leaching. For high grade ore, the traditional process still has advantages in capital and operating cost and valuable metals recovery, especially in precious metals recovery. INCO have built a demonstration plant with a pressure leaching process to treat Voisey`s Bay concentrate. The plant was started up in 2005. So far limited information has been released. Bioheap leaching has been applied successfully in the treatment of secondary copper ore. It treats crushed ore, avoiding the need for grinding and concentration steps. This in turn leads to cost savings which allows the processing of lower grade nickel sulphide and complex nickel sulphide resources which may currently be uneconomic to exploit. Many studies have been carried out in treating nickel sulphide. Titan has done pilot plant tests. The studies on bioheap leaching to treat nickel sulphide in China started in 2000. Laboratory and pilot plant tests have been done. And the process has been used at commercial scale. ###### 3.1. ###### ABSTRACT 

The aim of the trial heap leach project is to prove and demonstrate, both the technical and economic success of the leachability of the Зaldağ Nickel laterites by the atmospheric heap leach method (AHL) using dilute sulphuric acid and to produce saleable Nickel products from the leach liquor. 

Although the leachability of Balkan Nickel laterites is known, there has been no large scale plant constructed and operated for commercial AHL production until the application by European Nickel in Turkey. 

Three heaps and a small precipitation plant, producing 2 nickel cobalt hydroxide products, were constructed and commissioned in the trial period. The first heap was prepared to the represent the average of Зaldağ deposit (as known at the time) it was agglomerated using a dry polyacrylamide binder (Ciba Alcotec Fe10). Its leach period with some mini rinses and drainage cycles was completed after 548 days with the extractions of 79.4%, 82.7%, 30.0%, 78.9% and 37.1% for Nickel, Cobalt, Iron, Manganese and Aluminium respectively. The heap is currently undergoing its final rinse. 

Two nickel products have been produced, primary (24-35% Ni & 0.8-1.6% Co) and secondary (15-30% Ni, 0.5-1.0% Co & Mn 2.5%-11%) have been sold and shipped to various refineries for evaluation. 

In this paper, the general construction and commissioning of heap leach trial at Зaldağ, Turkey, the first heap AHL performance, its leach kinetics and also some operation performance issues of the precipitation circuit are presented.

###### 1. INTRODUCTION 

The exploration, acquisition and process development of the nickel laterites deposits in Turkey and the Balkan Region are the principal activities of European Nickel and have been since 1999. 

Based on research of the sulphuric acid heap leaching ability of Balkan nickel laterites, the company has focused on atmospheric heap leach (AHL) process to develop and demonstrate a low cost metallurgical process to extract nickel through a heap leach operation. According to exploration studies on Зaldağ Nickel Laterites in Turkey, European Nickel decided to investigate and develop a heap leach operation to produce nickel at substantially lower cost than other producers. 

BHP Billiton Plc, the largest diversified resource company in the world, has 12.2 percent of European Nickel and has supported European Nickel with the technological development of heap leach treatment of nickel laterites since 2003. 

European Nickel mined approximately 20,000 dry tons of ore from the Зaldağ laterites and constructed heaps in early 2004, so that the techniques and economic benefits of nickel heap leaching of Зaldağ laterites could be proven as a low cost alternative to conven

tional nickel processing using the demonstration heap leach plant at Зaldağ, Turkey. 

###### 2. GENERAL 

EN owns and operates the mine and processing plant through its 100% owned, Turkish registered subsidiary, Bosphorus Nickel Madencilik Ticaret AŞ (BN). 

The Зaldağ mine is located near Turgutlu in western Turkey, 70 km from the port of Izmir. The mine is situated between 476 m and 932 m above sea level on the Зaldağ mountain, entirely on government Forestry Department Land, and in an area which is partially forested or covered by scrub vegetation

###### 3. HEAP LEACH AREA PREPARATION 

To demonstrate on a large scale atmospheric heap leach performance of Зaldağ Nickel Laterites, the earthworks and construction of three pads for heaps, their leach liquor ponds, one excess pond and 4 launders to transfer leach solution from heaps to ponds and the installation of 1.5mm HDPE layer(s) for the heap leach area was completed in September 2004. 

Pads and ponds had a 300mm clay layer which was compacted to 95% proctor. . The solution corridor was a concrete structure. Pads had a single and ponds a double layer of HDPE placed above the clay layer to prevent possible acid leakage. 

A Leak detection system for pads and ponds was installed between the clay layer and the 1.5mm HDPE layer. A second leak detection system was installed between the primary and secondary HDPE layers for the ponds. Followed by the emplacement of PLS collection system, 500mm of gravel was placed above collection system to assist free drainage of PLS. 

In parallel with the HDPE application, the acid storage area construction was executed. All three acid tanks were installed by the end of September.

###### 4. ACID TANK AREA & DELIVERY 

There are three 22 m<sup>3</sup> concentrated sulphuric acid tanks, which are constructed from carbon steel and coated externally with epoxy, in the acid storage area. 

98% concentrated Sulphuric Acid is delivered to the site by tankers and unloaded to the storage tanks in the acid area. The elevation between acid tanks and pond area is enough to allow acid flow to the ponds by gravity therefore concentrated acid is added directly from tanks to ponds through a HDPE pipe installed to each pond with a floating disperser, when necessary. 

The acid strength of the ponds during the leach operation has been adjusted to about 75 g/L and measured everyday using oxalate free acid titration method before and after acid dosing. 

###### 5. ORE PREPARATION & MATERIAL PROPERTIES 

Demonstration of AHL and leach kinetics of different ore types was performed by heap1 and heap3 and the neutralisation leach to reduce acid content of PLS plant feed and acid consumption in the heap leaching process was investigated and demonstrated by heap 2. 

The material for the Зaldağ Heap Leach Trial Heap1 and Heap2 was selected to be representative of the entire Зaldağ ore body in terms of chemical, mineral and rock type content for determination of leach kinetics which have been extrapolated for the whole deposit. The material for heap 3 is representative of the first material to be mined for full scale.. 

Laboratory test works show that the nickel grade is higher in the smaller particles of the ore. The ore was crushed to facilitate acid percolation and increase surface area for leaching. 

All material was screened and crushed to minus 30 mm and in the first and second heaps underwent agglomeration. The coarse material over 30 mm was discarded. The crushed ore, after adding 0.8 kg/t of dry polyacrylamide binder (Ciba Alcotec Fe10) on the feed conveyor, was fed back to the agglomerator (60t/h capacity), water was added through spray nozzles in the agglomerator drum and all agglomerated ore was stacked after 24 hours air curing. 

Heap 3 was stacked unagglomerated as a result of positive column test work without agglomeration. Coarse material from 40 to100 mm was not discarded as in heaps 1 and 2 but was kept and used in the third heap to increase stability. 

A total of 3251 and 7519 dry tonnes of agglomerated ore were stacked to first and second heaps respectively, in the last quarter of 2004. The third heap was constructed with 8891 dry tonnes unagglomerated ore in May 2005. Heap 1 was 4 m high with heaps 2 and 3 stacked to 6 m high.

Red Limonite and Yellow Limonite zones are intercalated to each other. The main ore minerals are goethite and asbolane. As Red Limonite represents the most mature stage of natural leaching process, it is relatively poor in Ni and Co and high in Fe relative to Yellow Limonite. The asbolane amount in Yellow Limonite is higher than Red Limonite but goethite is still the main mineral of ore. All mineralogical studies indicate that Ni and Co are trappe

d in the crystal structure of goethite and asbolane. Weathered Serpentinite, refers to serpentine mineral, and is composed mainly of serpentine with asbolane being the main ore mineral. The term “saprolite” should be avoided as it is a given name to high clay bearing ores. This mineral has minor amounts of asbolane, clays (halloysite, montmorillonite, illite), garnierite and chlorite. The colour is yellowish to light green and well developed fractures are filled with clays and asbolane. The mineralogical analysis of the Зaldağ laterites indicates that goethite (Fe+3 O(OH)) is the dominant mineral which also traps more than 80% of Nickel in its crystal structure, serpentinite, quartz, calcite and other limonites are also predominant minerals whereas asbolane, clays and others are present in only minor amounts in the ore. ###### 7. HEAP LEACH OPERATION First irrigation was applied to Heap 1 on 18th October 2004, Heap 2 on 22nd February 2005 and Heap 3 on 19th May 2005. Instead of using open circuit operation, as applied in many Copper dilute sulphuric acid AHL processes, close circuit system has been used in this project. The flow diagram of the heap leach operation used in Зaldağ Project is shown in Figure 7-1. It is based on leach liquor metal concentration build-up in ponds through recirculation of the liquor on fresh ore. This process neutralises some of acid without losing any extracted Nickel and Cobalt before precipitating as a MHP product. This system helps reduce not only acid consumption and water usage in the main leach period but also decreases

limestone consumption in iron removal and neutralisation circuit in the precipitation operation. As can be seen in the flow diagram below, Heap 1 and Heap 3 have been irrigated continuously by Pond 1 and Pond 2 solutions respectively. Acid concentration of the solution has been adjusted to 75 g/L according to daily determination of the free acid in the solution; all heap underflow solutions have been collected in the launders and transferred to ponds, heaps or the precipitation plant. After 548 days of leach demonstration for heap 1 extractions of 79.4% Ni, 82.7% Co, 30.0% Fe, 78.9% Mn and 37.1% Al have been realized. 

To achieve approximately 80% Ni, Co and Mn extraction from heap 1, acid consumption has been calculated as 528 kg per ton dry ore according to flows in and out of the system. 

Following the 548 days (including drainage) of leaching for Heap 1, the heap is currently undergoing final rinse with a 10 g/L acidic solution, this is prepared using recycle water from the  precipitation plant. Once the nickel content of the solution underflow decreases the heap will be drained and then will be washed with water until the pH of the heap underflow liquor becomes about 7. The heap will then be decommissioned making way for further test heaps.

###### 8. PRECIPITATION PLANT 

To produce a saleable Nickel/Cobalt concentrate cake, the low acid pregnant leach solution (LA PLS) is processed in the precipitation plant. The precipitation construction commenced in September 2004 and was commissioned with LA PLS in March 2005. Figure 8-1 represents the process plant flow sheet. 

Figure 8-1 Precipitation Plant Flow Sheet 















As seen from Figure 8-1, the process plant has three main steps as follows; 

1. Iron Removal and Acid Neutralisation 

2. First Stage Nickel Precipitation 

3. Second Stage Nickel Precipitation. 

There are various precipitation parameters in the plant. The key parameter is pH and it is adjusted by limestone addition in iron removal circuit and by soda ash in the first and second stage of nickel precipitation circuit, all operation is at ambient conditions. 

The LA PLS feed to the iron removal circuit has a 24 hours residence time with 7 precipitation tanks. The aim of this circuit is to remove iron, aluminium & other impuities prior to the nickel circuis. 

The precipitated iron hydroxide, gypsum, aluminium hydroxide and other impurities are settled in an iron thickener using flocculant, the iron thickener overflow feeds the first stage Nickel precipitation tanks. The underflow is filtered using a vacuum belt filter to produce iron cake. 

The first stage Nickel precipitation circuit uses sodium carbonate solution with 8 hours residence time and a pH of 7.5, the slurry is settled in the nickel thickener. The underflow of the thickener is fed to a filter press and then Primary Nickel Product (PNP) is produced. The overflow is sent to the second stage of the nickel circuit where it has 4 hours residence time with 2 precipitation tanks at pH 8.5. The procedure of the second stage is as same as the first stage. So the settled Secondary Nickel Product (SNP) is also filtered by the filter press. All Nickel products are pachaged in bulk bags to be stored in the process plant area befo

ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### 9. CONCLUSION Turkey and Balkan laterites are amenable to heap leaching due to very low amount of clay contents. The Зaldağ Nickel leach characteristic have now been demonstrated in a large scale pilot plant by European Nickel. The leach period of the trial heaps has been monitored and leach kinetics have shown that there are three phases in the leach cycle, neutralisation, primary and secondary leach stages. In the neutralisation period, the first 12 days of acid treatment, Calcium precipitates as gypsum. Magnesium extracts with a high rate, as high as 20%. Nickel, Cobalt, Iron, Aluminium and Manganese begin to extract but with slower rates. After neutralisation period, the extraction rate of Nickel and Cobalt increases while iron magnesium, and aluminium have lower or steady state extraction. This higher extraction for Nickel and Cobalt after initial neutralisation resulted in this stage being named primary leach. In this stage extraction of Nickel, Cobalt, Iron, Aluminium and Manganese reached up to 23.4%, 16.7%, 0.08%, 1.25% and 10.2%, respectively for heap 1. In the secondary stage, which started on 76th day of leaching, all metals have constant leach rates which differ from the primary leach. Nickel, Cobalt, Iron, Aluminium and Manganese have achieved extraction of 79.4%, 84.7%, 29.1%, 37.0% and 76.0%, respectively after this stage of leaching. The Chromium has lowest extraction with 7% in whole leach perio

d. 

The acid consumption for neutralisation, primary and secondary stages per ton of dry or has been calculated as 35 kg, 116 kg and 377 kg. This resulted in approximate 80% extraction of Nickel where, a total of 510 kg per ton of dry ore was calculated for 72% extraction. 

The final stage of the demonstration plant is the precipitation area where the nickel cobalt hydroxide product is produced from pregnant leach liquor, with 33% Nickel and 1.5% Cobalt. The product has been shipped to various refineries worldwide for evaluation. 

The demonstration plant at Зaldağ has proved that Nickel and Cobalt can be extracted by means of atmospheric heap leaching and that saleable product can be produced.
